detail.abstract: A firm can read its AI bill in model usage and dollars and its labor bill in salaries and headcount, but comparing the two takes more than placing token prices beside wages. This paper sets out that comparison. It defines the cost per accepted task, which charges an AI system for inference, tools, human review, retries and the errors that slip through, and compares it with the same quantity for a human worker. It then derives when the comparison flips, how many tasks per year are needed to cover fixed overhead, and why a saving on tasks does not become a saving on positions until freed time can be pooled into whole jobs. In an illustrative calibration with four assumed task classes, AI has a lower modeled cost per accepted task in all four before a quality constraint is imposed. Exception resolution and code repair have higher residual error rates than their human baselines, so their cost advantage has to be read together with a human-parity quality floor. The margin is narrow for exception resolution, and the advantage there disappears at half the assumed wage, when each retry's success rate falls to 60 percent of the previous attempt's, when review wrongly rejects one fifth of correct outputs, or when an AI error costs 1.5 times a human one. Inference is between 2.5 and 24 percent of AI cost, so wages, review, detection and error cost matter more than the price of inference. In the cost-only calibration, an illustrative team of ten releases time equivalent to 6.1 FTEs, and the assumed pooling rule turns that capacity into four whole-position reductions. When the human-parity quality floor is imposed, the time released falls to 5.2 FTEequivalents; four positions remain removable at N = 10, but the reduction falls from nine to eight at N = 20 and from 29 to 24 at N = 60. These are conditional model results, not predictions of actual employment changes. Quality floors and tail-risk limits can change which workflow is feasible, and whether a tail limit excludes AI depends on whether the human team shares the shock. All numerical results are conditional on assumed inputs. The paper closes with a protocol for replacing these assumptions with measured values.

detail.abstract: The purpose of this research is to determine the customer satisfaction in the call centers of Karachi considering the call centers of mobile network service provider. To evaluate customer satisfaction, five independent variables are taken which includes availability of service, service quality, completeness of service, professionalism, and responsiveness. Quantitative research method has been applied, for this a questionnaire is designed to collect data. The study involves 384 participants and the data was collected from Karachi. Reliability, Factor Analysis with Principle Component method and Multiple Regression Analysis were applied to test the proposed hypothesis. The findings show that continuous improvements on availability of service, service quality, and completeness of service have positive impact on customer satisfaction and the relationships of these variables with the dependent variable are statistical significant. Professionalism, and responsiveness are found insignificant in predicting customer satisfaction in the call centers of Karachi. This study benefits the call center managers to better understand those factors which help the customers to satisfy with the call center service.

detail.abstract: Firms are increasingly treating consumer privacy as a strategic asset, but it remains unclear whether voluntary privacy efforts, as part of a privacy stewardship strategy, lead to greater customer acquisition. Since consumers cannot directly verify data-handling practices, privacy acts as a credence attribute whose value depends on effective intermediaries and operational maturity. We analyze a U.S. auto insurer's 2013 policy change on their innovative Usage Based Insurance (UBI) program that enhanced privacy by discontinuing the storage of customer location data. We do this by using a natural experiment created by a staggered state-level program rollout. Studying 131,874 consumers' enrollment decisions across 14 states, we find that privacy enhancement has a greater impact on UBI adoption in markets where the program is more mature, what we call the marginal barrier principle: privacy becomes a key obstacle once other, primarily operational, issues are increasingly resolved. This effect is especially strong in the specialist-agent channel, which focuses on auto insurance, and is almost three times more effective than generalist agents who sell a wide range of insurance products. Our findings show that capable intermediation can be crucial for establishing privacy protection as a marketable attribute, extending privacy research beyond online settings to traditional markets.

detail.abstract: Sustainable New Product Introductions (SNPIs) enable firms to meet consumers’ increasing demand for sustainable options while addressing rising expectations for corporate environmental responsibility. This study demonstrates that SNPIs can also strengthen brands by enhancing brand equity. Drawing on signaling theory, we propose that SNPIs serve as product-based sustainability signals that enhance brand equity by generating social goodwill. A staggered event study of the initial launch of a sustainable product line by a major laundry detergent brand shows that SNPIs can increase parent-brand equity. A complementary analysis of subsequent SNPIs across 15 leading brands in 12 retail chains reveals that this effect is moderated by parent firms' ethical reputation and retail chains' sustainable assortment share. These findings advance our understanding of whether and under what conditions sustainable products serve as credible signals of environmental responsibility and enhance brand equity.

title: Behind The Model Name: Identification and Access Barriers in Published Studies of Language Model Behavior

detail.abstract: Studies of language model behavior are cited as if they described a stable object. The object changes. I audited 64 behavioral studies published from 2023 to September 2026 in six science journals and seven marketing journals. Of the 62 papers that studied at least one closed model, 90 to 94 percent studied a configuration that could not be requested on 26 September 2026 or that the paper does not identify. After the shutdowns announced for 23 October 2026, 79 percent will have no closed configuration left that is identifiable and still served. Only 34 to 37 percent identify every closed model they used. These figures count barriers to a repeat, not failed repeats. To see what a repeat can show, I registered a successor check of Goli and Singh (2024) before the first query and ran it on five systems. The original model gave English estimates close to those of 2023. Four current systems chose the later reward 34 to 73 percentage points more often. For three of them the share shifted by 16 to 20 points between two runs that differed in the order of the options and in the day. A finding about a model name therefore needs a date, an identifier and a record of what was held fixed. I list the facts that a paper needs to report so that a later study can compare like with like.

detail.abstract: Clothing functions not only as a form of aesthetic expression but also as a medium through which individuals manage self-presentation and regulate social visibility. Among Generation Z, oversized clothing has emerged as a prominent fashion trend; however, its psychological implications remain relatively underexplored. The present study investigates the relationship between self-concealment and oversized clothing behaviour among Generation Z college students. A quantitative research design was employed, and data were collected from 456 college students using standardized measures, including the Self-Concealment Scale (Larson & Chastain, 1990) and the Oversized Clothing Behaviour Scale for Gen Z college Students, prepared & standardized by the investigator & the supervisor. Statistical analyses such as descriptive analysis, independent sample t-test, one-way ANOVA, and Pearson correlation were used to examine differences and relationships among the study variables. The findings indicated no significant differences in oversized clothing behaviour and selfconcealment based on gender and age groups. However, significant differences were observed based on the primary reasons for wearing oversized clothing. Correlation analysis revealed a moderate positive relationship between oversized clothing behaviour and self-concealment (r = .466, p < .001), suggesting that individuals with higher tendencies toward self-concealment are more likely to engage in oversized clothing behaviour. The study highlights that clothing choices may serve as subtle behavioural expressions of underlying psychological tendencies. Understanding such associations contributes to a broader perspective on appearance-related behaviours, self-presentation, and psychological processes among young adults.

detail.abstract: As mortgage shopping moves online, lenders gain data on borrowers' search and browsing activity. These data improve screening, lower rates, and expand credit. But they also support targeted advertising that reduces comparison shopping and raises markups. Which force dominates determines who benefits from online data. I exploit the staggered adoption of state privacy laws limiting these uses, comparing borrowers at the same lender across states. Restricting data lowers mortgage rates by 14 basis points at advertising-reliant lenders: lower markups outweigh weaker screening. Consistent with weaker screening, approval rates fall one percentage point for credit scores below 750 and rise half a point above it. Consistent with weaker targeting, paid-search clicks fall 7% at lenders using advertising-platform data. A search model shows that privacy shifts surplus from lenders to borrowers but reduces total surplus because search becomes costlier and screening weaker. In digital lending, data-use rules shape search and credit access.

detail.abstract: Software-defined networking (SDN) separates the control plane from the data plane and exposes a logically centralized, programmable view of network state. This architecture creates a natural setting for data-driven control, yet most production controllers still rely on static policies, heuristics, or analytically tractable optimization models that struggle with volatile traffic and heterogeneous service requirements. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an alternative: an agent learns resource-allocation policies through interaction with the network, guided by a reward signal rather than labelled examples. This paper reviews the peer-reviewed literature on RL-based resource orchestration in SDN, covering routing and traffic engineering, network slicing, and cross-domain resource management. We organize existing work by learning paradigm, orchestration task, and deployment assumptions, and we compare value-based, policy-gradient, actor-critic, multi-agent, and model-augmented approaches. The review identifies recurring gaps: dependence on simulation, weak treatment of safety during exploration, limited generalization across topologies, scalability of centralized agents, and the absence of standardized benchmarks. We then propose a conceptual, layered framework that combines graphbased state representation, constrained policy learning, and hierarchical multi-agent coordination, together with a staged validation pathway. The framework is presented as a research agenda, not as an implemented or validated system. The paper closes with practical implications for operators and directions for future work. No new experiments are reported; all empirical claims are attributed to the cited sources.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an operational backbone for contemporary business promotion rather than a peripheral experiment. This working paper examines how recommendation systems, generative content tools, conversational agents, and programmatic advertising platforms are reshaping the ways firms attract, engage, and retain customers. Drawing on recent large-scale industry surveys from McKinsey, Salesforce, HubSpot and related research bodies, together with established theoretical perspectives in marketing science, the paper charts the progression from rule-based segmentation to continuous, individual-level optimization and, more recently, toward agentic systems capable of multi-step campaign execution. Measured benefits in personalization, content throughput, and service efficiency are set against a persistent gap between tool adoption and workflow redesign, as well as against ethical, regulatory, and labor-market pressures. Particular attention is given to the emerging compliance environment shaped by the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and the expanding set of state-level rules in the United States. The central argument is that sustainable advantage will depend less on the volume of AI tools deployed and more on the quality of governance, measurement discipline, and human oversight that organizations build around those tools.

detail.abstract: The rapid growth of social networking sites has created new opportunities for communication, information sharing, marketing, and community development. However, these platforms have also become attractive environments for spam accounts, fraudulent activities, phishing messages, malicious links, and misleading content. Traditional spam detection techniques often depend on predefined rules, manually selected features, and conventional machine learning algorithms. Although these methods can identify familiar spam patterns, their performance may decline when malicious users modify their behavior or develop new strategies to avoid detection. Deep learning offers an alternative by learning complex patterns from textual content, user behavior, account characteristics, and relationships between users. This article examines the application of deep learning approaches to detecting spam accounts and malicious content on social networking sites. It discusses convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory networks, transformer-based models, and graph neural networks, emphasizing their respective strengths and limitations. The article also presents a proposed detection framework that combines content analysis, behavioral profiling, and social network relationships. Evaluation considerations, including precision, recall, F1-score, computational efficiency, and resistance to changing spam patterns, are discussed. The analysis suggests that combining multiple sources of evidence can provide a more comprehensive approach to social media threat detection. Nevertheless, practical deployment requires careful attention to data quality, privacy, fairness, explainability, and the consequences of incorrectly classifying legitimate users.

title: The Visibility Tax: Why Fmcg Companies Are Spending More To Stand Still

detail.title: The Visibility Tax: Why Fmcg Companies Are Spending More To Stand Still

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No funding. Self Funded
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract:
The fundamental economic engine of the Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) sector is undergoing a profound structural transformation. For decades, the industry’s growth playbook was linear and predictable: build brand equity, secure physical distribution, stimulate demand, and capture scale economies. In this traditional model, marketing was viewed as a strategic investment in future demand, while trade spend was a lever to drive incremental volume. Today, this model is becoming increasingly untenable.

As consumer journeys fragment across physical stores, marketplaces, social commerce, and ultra-fast delivery apps, retailers and digital platforms are aggressively monetizing access to these audiences. Consequently, brands are no longer merely paying for physical distribution; they are increasingly forced to pay for discoverability within that distribution. We term this emerging structural friction the Visibility Tax.

The Visibility Tax represents the escalating commercial expenditure an FMCG company must deploy simply to preserve its existing baseline of visibility, search ranking, digital shelf presence, and market share amid intensifying channel monetization.

detail.abstract: The paper states its wager at maximum strength and immediately makes it falsifiable: preference for a sign may begin below culture, below rationality, and below branding itself—in a sub-second event of contour processing by the visual cortex. If so, sign geometry is a primary foundation of pricing power; if not, the thesis is dead, and this paper is designed to record that result first. The test is an isolated choice system involving two physically and functionally identical products that differ only in the contour of the sign: the thought result 900/100 has a two-sided binomial probability of approximately 1.34e-161 under the null hypothesis and would mean that contour carries a choice variable prior to any rational comparison.

detail.abstract: Soaring prices of NFT digital art have sparked growing scholarly and public interest, raising questions about whether valuations reflect systematic fundamentals or speculative excess. This paper investigates what explains price formation in the NFT market using transactions from the CryptoPunks collectible market involving 3,230 unique traders. Leveraging the full observability of blockchain data, we estimate hedonic pricing models with progressively richer fixed-effect structures, culminating in a within-seller specification that identifies price effects from variation in individual seller behavior over time. Three findings emerge. First, the seller side carries the bulk of the identified within-trader pricing variation in a way that cross-sectional models conceal: seller experience is negatively associated with prices across sellers but positively associated within a seller over time, reflecting a learning effect; seller trading frequency reverses from positive to steeply negative once within-seller variation is isolated, corresponding to an 82.2% price reduction. Buyer characteristics play a comparatively limited role. Second, statistical rarity is priced uniformly across participants, while visual rarity, a pixel-level measure of aesthetic distinctiveness, is trader-mediated. Its premium attenuates when trader fixed effects absorb persistent valuation tendencies, revealing that visual effects in cross-sectional models partly reflect who trades rather than what is traded. Third, past comparable peak prices and recent trading activity anchor current transaction prices, but these effects attenuate substantially once trader composition is controlled for, indicating that market-condition sensitivity in standard hedonic models partly proxies for time-varying participation. Together, the findings highlight that trader composition is not merely a control variable in NFT valuation models; it materially affects the estimated pricing relationships.

detail.abstract: AI marketing makes shopping harder to resist. AI adds a fast feedback loop. Recommendations can change as you search, pause, click, scroll, or leave something in your basket. Personalised marketing works partly because relevance saves mental effort. Instead of comparing hundreds of options, shoppers receive a small selection that seems made for them. Repetition creates familiarity, reviews provide social reassurance, and scarcity messages give people a reason to act now. The risk is not that AI removes free choice. It can shorten the gap between wanting something and considering whether it is needed. That can encourage unplanned purchases, unnecessary upgrades and products bought mainly because the opportunity feels urgent. Mindfulness may help. Applied to shopping, that means interrupting the familiar script. Mindful consumption through three connected ideas: awareness of what shapes a choice; care for its effects on ourselves, society, and the environment; and temperance or recognising when enough is enough. Before a non-essential purchase, ask: did I plan to buy this before I saw the recommendation? What need will it meet? How often will I use it? What might this product replace—or become when I no longer want it? Then create a little friction. Leave the item in your basket for a day. Turn off retail notifications, remove stored payment details and shop from a list rather than an endless recommendation feed. Check whether a recommendation is sponsored and compare it with options outside the platform that suggested it.

title: Bringing Products Closer: Object–Environment Relations in Augmented Reality and Their Effects on Psychological Distance and Preferences

detail.abstract: Brands such as IKEA and Amazon allow consumers to explore products through Augmented Reality (AR) in their own immediate environments. Drawing on visual-scene processing and psychological distance, this research argues that AR enhances consumer preference for products by reducing psychological distance, i.e., how close the product is to one’s immediate experience. This effect, however, depends on the relation between the product displayed in AR and the environment in which it appears. Modifying Biederman, Mezzanotte, and Rabinowitz’s (1982) work on relational violations, we conceptualize five AR-inherent product-environment relations of how products in AR can physically or semantically violate their relation to the environment, thereby increasing psychological distance and reducing preferences (e.g., purchase intention, attitudes, or willingness-to-pay). While physical violations also impact the concept of presence (i.e., whether the object feels real), semantic violations affect psychological distance without necessarily impacting presence. Eight main experiments and five replications (NTotal = 7,477) support our propositions. Managerially, our findings mean that while AR can positively impact consumer preferences, its effectiveness depends on guiding consumers toward appropriate object placement, offering insights for AR interface design and online retail strategy.

detail.abstract: Language-model extraction of ESG data is scored against human references that are often revised after the model has run, yet those revisions are seldom versioned or measured. We propose a versioned gold-standard protocol: a blind reference fixed before extraction, every later revision logged with its page evidence and trigger, identical predictions scored against every version, and a worst-case headline. We apply it to 36 stratified Hang Seng Index constituents (396 cells, eleven headline fields). Revisions prompted by model disagreement change 22 cells, 21 toward the model, and raise measured accuracy by 5.1 percentage points with the predictions unchanged. Against the blind reference, a BM25-plus-LLM pipeline scores 90.9% (firm-bootstrap 95% CI 87.1-93.9%) on the 24 firms annotated fully blind and never used in prompt development, and 90.7% on all 36 (89.6% under the pre-specified unit normaliser). A generic regex-and-table heuristic scores 35.6%. Retrieval placed the gold evidence page in the model's context for 98% of disclosed cells, including every missed or wrong value that has a cited page. Under the written prompt, only two of the 37 errors are model errors, plus one masked by an identical gold error. The rest are gold omissions, prompt-gold specification conflicts, definitional ambiguity and unverifiable disclosure. For this reasoning model, residual error arises after retrieval, in the definition of the target; a partial comparison suggests a weaker model loses about ten points. ESG extraction accuracy is a property of a model and a reference together, and benchmarks should report both.

detail.abstract: We study joint assortment selection and personalized pricing under a mixture of multinomial logit models, and extend this setting to include inventory decisions. In the assortment setting, the seller first selects a cardinality-constrained set of products with unlimited supply; after observing each customer's type, it then customizes both the offered subset and its prices. We develop a sales-based fluid relaxation with rounding-aware constraints and round it using pivotal sampling, whose weak negative regression property yields a 1/2-approximation. This improves the best known guarantee for joint assortment selection and personalized pricing and removes an ϵ loss in the fixed-price case, in which only the offered subset is customized. The factor 1/2 is tight relative to our relaxation. For the inventory extension, the seller chooses integer initial inventories under a total-unit capacity and, over a finite horizon, customizes offered subsets and prices as customers arrive and inventory depletes. Pivotal sampling rounds the fractional inventory to a stocking plan that respects the capacity in every realization. Specialized online contention resolution schemes and a menu lottery then yield the first 1/4-approximation for this setting. When prices are fixed, greedy acceptance improves the guarantee to (1-1/e)/2, removing the ϵ loss from the best known bound.

detail.abstract: The transition from academic life to professional employment exposes interns to unfamiliar responsibilities, performance expectations, interpersonal challenges, and workplace demands. This study examines self-reported mental toughness, workplace experiences, behavioural characteristics, and burnout-related experiences among 51 interns working in consulting, product management, and marketing/business roles. The research uses a cross-sectional survey containing 40 five-point Likert-scale statements and two categorical questions. The overall mental toughness composite was 3.27 out of 5. Confidence recorded the highest mean among the four mental toughness dimensions (M = 3.43), followed by adaptability (M = 3.29), resilience (M = 3.20), and stress tolerance (M = 3.14). Among workplace factors, managerial support received the highest mean (M = 3.44), while feedback quality received the lowest (M = 3.22). Self-efficacy (M = 3.55) and growth mindset (M = 3.50) were the highest-scoring behavioural constructs. The burnout-related composite averaged 3.42, with anxiety about work recording the highest mean among the four distress indicators (M = 3.53). Descriptive comparisons showed differences across internship roles and work arrangements. Consulting interns reported the highest burnout-related mean, while remote interns reported the highest average mental toughness and psychological safety scores. These patterns are exploratory and do not establish causal effects or statistically significant differences. The study contributes an intern-focused descriptive account of psychological resources and workplace experiences and identifies areas for future investigation, including feedback practices, role clarity, workload pressure, and the relationship between perceived capability and workplace distress.

detail.abstract: Whether Europe has fallen behind the United States and China is central to European economic policy, yet the debate pools very different activities into one verdict. This study separates three stages of technological competitiveness: knowledge (the science base), creation (turning knowledge into firms, capital, frontier technology and exportable manufacturing) and deployment (adoption and diffusion). It measures the European Union's position in business, artificial intelligence and renewable energy against both rivals with 14 indicators from six public sources. Each indicator is expressed as a log ratio and analysed with HAC-robust trend tests, a pre-specified test for a change after 2020 and leave-one-out pillar indices. In 2023 the EU stood at 1.34 times the United States in knowledge and 1.23 times in deployment, but at 0.33 in creation. Against China it stood at 0.55, 0.29 and 1.52, respectively, and all three ratios declined by 4-12% a year from 2017. The EU's share of R&D among the world's 1,000 largest corporate investors fell from 24.7% to 16.4% between FY2010 and FY2024, and its share of ICT corporate R&D from 16.2% to 6.0%. Europe has fallen behind, but mainly in conversion rather than in science or adoption.

detail.abstract: Organizations deploying AI agents commonly report that they learn what their agents did only after the fact. This paper sets out how to measure that claim, and makes the measurement available to any operator of LibreChat, a widely used open-source chat and agent platform. From prior work on delegation as an intellectual capability we derive a delegated-task specification: a delegation is governed when it names an accountable owner, bounds the task and the systems the agent may reach, states what the agent must never do, defines an escalation path, and remains reviewable after it changes. We operationalize the specification as a read-only audit that runs against a deployment's database and emits aggregate counts only. It measures whether agent lifecycle events are recorded at all, how much agent activity ran on agents that have since been deleted, how often agents changed while other people could use them, and how often agents hold capability with no stated bounds. Its headline measures are structural and do not depend on the language in which agents are instructed, so results are comparable across deployments in any country; keyword-based measures are reported separately as English-only. We describe a multi-site protocol under which each operator runs the audit on its own system and shares only the resulting counts, and we state the analysis plan and expected findings before any multi-site data are collected. Results from the first site, and from participating universities and organizations, will follow in a revision of this paper and in a companion multi-site paper.

detail.abstract:
Ukraine's economic independence after the war will depend less on how much external support it receives than on the terms, timing and accountability attached to that support. This policy paper examines how wartime financing can be turned into lasting fiscal capacity without creating obligations that narrow future policy choices.

Between February 2022 and August 2026, Ukraine's budget received about USD 196 billion in external financing, increasingly as loans, including G7 ERA loans serviced from revenues on immobilised Russian assets and a EUR 90 billion EU Support Loan to be repaid from reparations. Recent debt operations reduce near-term risk but defer rather than cancel obligations, which cluster in 2029-2032 and 2035-2039. Public debt reached 107.1% of GDP in 2025, and defence and security spending is budgeted at about 42% of GDP in 2026.

The paper compares Ukraine with 17 post-conflict recoveries across about 30 indicators. Ukraine's profile is closest, though only moderately, to Ethiopia after 1998-2000, Lebanon after 1975-1990 and Vietnam after 1976. In these cases government effectiveness improved gradually, the defence burden remained the largest drag on recovery, the effect of external agreements on sovereignty worsened in the first five years of reconstruction, and debt sustainability worsened again 11-20 years on as deferred obligations fell due. These are associations from a small historical sample, not forecasts. The paper closes with nine recommendations, each with its trade-offs.

detail.abstract: Throughout human history, extraordinary internal states-ranging from mystical revelations and visions to near-death experiences-have served as foundational catalysts for cultural cosmologies, religious dogmas, and sociopolitical frameworks (James 1902). While the raw, felt reality of these phenomenological events is unquestioned by the individual, their epistemological validity remains subject to critical dispute (Plantinga 1993; Nozick 1981). This paper formalizes "The Experience-Truth Gap," analysing the frequent conflation of subjective certainty (conviction) with objective reality (truth). Drawing upon decision science, cognitive psychology, and analytical epistemology, this study proposes a three-tier model of empirical evaluation: Phenomenological Observation, Interpretive Framing, and Empirical Verification. Ultimately, this paper argues that while subjective experience possesses existential and psychological validity, it lacks intrinsic diagnostic force for objective claims. The principle of Strategic Truth is advanced as a method to mitigate cognitive biases in high-stakes epistemic assessments (Kahneman 2011; Stanovich 2004).

detail.abstract: This paper argues that Namibia has been, across 175 years, a constitutive site of knowledge production whose benefits accrued overwhelmingly to external institutions while its internal capability base was systematically depleted. Francis Galton's 1850-52 expedition to South West Africa was not a prelude to his scientific career but a formative episode in the development of hereditary theory, biometry, regression analysis, and the nature-nurture debate. The intellectual chain from Galton's fieldwork to Eugen Fischer's Namibian racial anthropometry to Nazi racial law, and the accompanying physical extraction of Namibian human remains to institutions in Berlin, Vienna, Strasbourg, Zurich, and New York, constitute a political economy of knowledge extraction structurally parallel to the colonial extraction of minerals and labor from the same territory. Against this history the paper develops a rationalized endogenous growth model that formalizes the complementarity between general and indigenous technological knowledge, connects an event history of biological extraction, institutional recognition, and repatriation to the dynamics of indigenous knowledge accumulation, and derives the policy implication that Namibia's green hydrogen and artificial intelligence prospects depend on raising the share of resource rents directed toward indigenous knowledge and human capital-reversing a colonial design that kept that share at zero.

detail.abstract: Background,Professional growth and perceived compensation and benefits are potentially modifiable organizational resources, but their relationships with dimensions of burnout remain unclear. This study examines how professional growth and perceived compensation and benefits relate to exhaustion and disengagement, the energetic and motivational dimensions of burnout, respectively, among nursing staff in U.S. health centers.,Methods,This cross-sectional study used data from a nationally administered workforce well-being survey at Health Resources and Services Administration–supported health centers in the U.S. The analytic sample included 5,652 nursing staff: 3,855 nurses, 1,691 nurse practitioners, and 106 nurse aides or assistants. Exploratory and ordinal confirmatory factor analyses in separate subsamples examined exhaustion and disengagement using 16 burnout items. Separate multivariable linear regression models examined associations of professional growth, perceived compensation and benefits, and their interaction with each burnout dimension. Models adjusted for five additional workplace constructs and respondent and health center characteristics, using HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. A secondary latent profile analysis characterized workplace patterns across seven standardized constructs. Differences in exhaustion and disengagement across profiles were assessed using the Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars procedure to account for classification uncertainty. Several sensitivity analyses to examine the robustness of the primary results.,Results,Among 5,652 nursing staff, psychometric analyses favored separate exhaustion and disengagement dimensions over a single burnout factor. In fully adjusted models, professional growth was statistically significantly associated with lower disengagement (β = -0.247, 95% CI [-0.272, -0.221], p < .001) but was not associated with exhaustion (p = .070). Perceived compensation and benefits were statistically significantly associated with lower exhaustion (β = -0.048, 95% CI [-0.073, -0.024], p < .001) but not with disengagement (p = .381). The professional-growth-by-compensation interaction was not statistically significant for exhaustion (p = .315) but was for disengagement (β = 0.019, 95% CI [-0.036, -0.003], Holm-adjusted p = .047). Professional growth was also associated with lower disengagement across the observed compensation range. Secondary latent profile analysis identified four workplace resource-strain profiles: high-resource/low-strain (19.8%), moderate-resource/near-average-strain (52.1%), low-resource/high-strain (22.6%), and very-low-resource/very-high-strain (5.6%). Exhaustion and disengagement were progressively higher in profiles with fewer resources and greater strain. Sensitivity analyses supported the primary regression findings, whereas profile assignments were sensitive to covariance assumptions and largely reflected a continuous workplace resource-strain gradient.,Conclusion,Professional growth was associated with lower disengagement, and perceived compensation and benefits with lower exhaustion, suggesting organizational strategies tailored to distinct burnout dimensions among nursing staff in U.S. health centers.

detail.abstract: Yuen Yuen Ang introduces Adaptive Industrial Policy as an approach to governing innovation when governments cannot know in advance which industries will succeed. Drawing on Adaptive Political Economy, which treats societies as complex rather than complicated and takes uncertainty rather than risk as its starting point, Ang challenges the false binary between neoliberalism and interventionism. Neither adequately addresses a world shaped by deglobalization, AI disruption, uncertain growth engines, and national-security-driven industrial policy in which everything becomes a priority. Her concept of Directed Improvisation explains how governments can influence rather than dictate outcomes by structuring variation, selection, retention, and niche creation. Through Meta-Institutions such as Adaptive Policy Communication, governments combine clear directives with ambiguous signals, establishing guardrails while enabling experimentation, flexible implementation, and feedback. This approach reflects a signal economy rather than a command economy and can be studied empirically: Ang and co-authors use large language models to analyze clear and ambiguous signals across millions of central government instructions. Ang illustrates the approach through China’s e-commerce industry, which the government did not pick as a winner in advance but discovered and supported over time, evolving from benign neglect to infrastructure building to “suffocating love.” She concludes that uncertainty is not a bug but a feature of twenty-first-century policymaking, requiring new approaches to industrial policy and a research and training ecosystem built for uncertainty.

detail.abstract: Climate-related psychological strain is an emerging HRM concern, yet its relationship with employee engagement remains underexplored. This study develops and refines the Eco-Anxiety and Workplace (Dis)Engagement (EWD) framework using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, combining quantitative data from 182 private-sector employees with interviews with 10 participants. Findings show that substantial eco-anxiety can coexist with high employee engagement, challenging assumptions that climate concern necessarily leads to disengagement. The proposed framework comprises two related dimensions: psychosocial and organisational, neither of which uniquely predicted engagement when modelled simultaneously. Qualitative findings highlight agency, meaning, value congruence and perceived organisational authenticity as potential mechanisms shaping workplace outcomes. The study reframes eco-anxiety as a contextual HRM challenge and extends engagement and Job Demands–Resources perspectives by emphasising the role of credible, actionable organisational resources in shaping how climate-related strain is experienced at work.

detail.abstract: In stochastic control problems involving optimal portfolio choice, one often seeks an optimizer of some local criterion (dynamic programming value function) generated by some global criterion (e.g., expected utility). The local optimizer then typically acts as a stochastic integrand with respect to some multi-variate stochastic process (e.g., asset prices). This paper takes a closer look at local criteria in the form of "local expected utility". Since the existence of the local optimizer can be established under very mild conditions, it is crucial to understand under what circumstances the local optimizer has good integrability properties. It is shown that the reasonable asymptotic elasticity condition of Kramkov and Schachermayer applied to the local utility function plays a key role in this context.

detail.abstract: We explain the coexistence of stock and mutual organizational forms and their relative dominance in different insurance markets in a market equilibrium model. Organizational forms endogenously reflect the benefits and costs of equity, and the impact of insurer operating efficiencies. Stock insurers are larger and more efficient than mutual insurers. Mutualization (i) increases with taxes and agency costs; (ii) decreases with the mean and idiosyncratic variability of insuree losses; (iii) increases with aggregate insurer asset and liability risks; (iv) increases (decreases) with the market return when insuree loss variance is low (high). Evidence from U.S. insurance data supports all our predictions.

detail.abstract: Innovation has become central to debates on industrialisation, technological change and sustainable development. Yet the capacity to innovate remains unevenly distributed, and the adoption of advanced technologies does not necessarily generate endogenous productive capabilities, institutional autonomy or ecological resilience. These challenges are particularly consequential for African economies seeking to move beyond commodity dependence and strengthen their participation in global value chains. This paper proposes Innovationology as a developing transdisciplinary research programme concerned with how societies generate, organise, adapt, evaluate and govern innovation across technological, economic, institutional, epistemic, cultural and socio-ecological systems. Drawing on established scholarship on innovation systems, transformative innovation policy, mission-oriented innovation and traditional ecological knowledge, the paper argues that innovation should be examined not merely as a measurable output or commercial activity, but as a systemic capability shaped by relationships among knowledge, power, institutions and environments. It develops a preliminary framework organised around five analytical dimensions: knowledge generation and integration, capability formation, institutional coordination and governance, epistemic agency and inclusion, and socio-ecological transformation. The framework is applied to Africa's sustainable industrial development, with particular attention to artificial intelligence, Indigenous knowledge, domestic value addition and regenerative resource systems. Recent research and policy assessments on African industrial policy, sustainability transitions and inclusive artificial intelligence help situate the proposal within contemporary debates (Ferraz et al., 2024; Ince, 2026). The paper concludes by outlining a research agenda involving conceptual clarification, comparative empirical investigation, context-sensitive indicators and policy experimentation. Innovationology is advanced as a research programme whose scientific contribution must be established through methodological transparency, empirical testing and critical engagement with existing disciplines.

detail.abstract: The language of "cyberwar" has become common in policy, media, and strategic debate, yet most hostile digital operations do not meet the legal or political threshold of war. They occur continuously, exploit civilian and military networks simultaneously, involve uncertain attribution, and pursue effects ranging from intelligence collection and coercion to disruption, pre-positioning, and influence. This article develops the concept of persistent technological conflict to describe this intermediate condition. The concept refers to sustained interstate and state-linked competition conducted through cyber operations, data infrastructures, artificial intelligence, supply chains, digital platforms, and technological dependencies, generally below the threshold of armed conflict but with cumulative consequences for sovereignty, security, and international order. Using qualitative analysis of academic literature, international legal frameworks, official threat assessments, and regulatory developments, the article distinguishes persistent technological conflict from cybercrime, technological competition, and cyberwar. It argues that cyberspace does not abolish the distinction between peace and war; rather, it makes that distinction harder to observe, attribute, and govern. The strategic response should therefore avoid both complacency and indiscriminate militarisation. Effective state cybersecurity requires resilience, proportionate attribution, public-private coordination, international norms, protection of civilian infrastructure, and equitable cyber-capacity development. The article concludes that contemporary international relations are increasingly characterised not by a declared global cyberwar, but by permanent technological contestation whose cumulative effects can prepare, accompany, or substitute for conventional force.

title: The Token Economy - How AI Process Utilities Will Displace Time-and-Material Billing in Enterprise Services

detail.abstract:
The professional services industry has, for decades, monetized cognitive work through a single dominant construct: the billable hour. Time-and-material contracts, FTE-based engagements, and headcount-driven delivery models have been the unchallenged architecture of enterprise service pricing — in consulting, technology implementation, legal services, and financial operations alike. This paper argues that this architecture is structurally obsolete, and that its displacement has already begun.

The emergence of large language models introduces a new atomic unit of enterprise cognitive work: the token. Unlike the labor-hour — which is opaque, variable, and impossible to standardize — the token is quantified, auditable, reproducible, and continuously improvable. This paper proposes that token-based delivery, governed by the principles of Lean Six Sigma process management, constitutes not merely an efficiency improvement over existing models but a categorical redefinition of how cognitive work is priced, delivered, and improved.

We introduce the concept of the AI Process Utility — an enterprise service provider that acquires AI model capacity at volume from foundation model providers, delivers that capacity through proprietary workflow architectures, and continuously optimizes consumption through structured prompt engineering. The central operating metric of this model — Tokens-Per-Quality-Outcome (TPQO) — serves as a direct analogue to classical process efficiency ratios, enabling the application of DMAIC methodology to AI-delivered knowledge work for the first time.

The paper further examines the financial architecture required to operationalize this model at scale: volume commitment deals with AI providers, loss-leader enterprise pricing funded by capital markets, and the compounding margin advantage created by proprietary prompt optimization history — a data moat invisible to competitors operating at the same nominal token price.

We identify the Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance sector as the primary near-term disruption surface, given its combination of high-volume repeatable cognitive tasks, regulatory appetite for auditability, and existing dependence on T&M outsourcing relationships with IT majors who are structurally constrained from self-disruption.

Finally, we examine the long-term value accumulation mechanism of the model — the Organizational Language Model (OLM) — wherein session data compounds into organization-specific AI context, creating switching costs and network effects that transform a pricing arbitrage play into a durable enterprise platform.

The thesis concludes that the transition from T&M to token-based billing is not a question of if, but of who executes it first, at what scale, and with sufficient process rigor to defend quality while compressing cost. The window for category creation is open. It will not remain so.

detail.abstract:
During the acceleration of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption across highly regulated sectors, enterprises face a critical governance vulnerability: the Actuator Gap. Traditional IT governance models rely on static perimeters; however, autonomous agentic systems execute tasks across multi-cloud environments at machine speed, transforming flawed legacy processes into immediate, kinetic operational liabilities. While telemetry and post-hoc audit logging provide necessary visibility, detection without automated intervention is insufficient to halt unauthorized machine execution.

This article presents a dual-pillar governance architecture that operationalizes the People, Process, and Technology (PPT) imperative. Grounded in the ISO/IEC 38500 Evaluate-Direct-Monitor (EDM) model and ISO/IEC 42001, the proposed framework introduces pipeline-native technical circuit breakers—utilizing Governance as Code (GaC), automated promotion gates, and real-time observability—to deterministically halt policy-violating agents. Concurrently, this model addresses the leadership bottleneck through Systemic Risk Stewardship, redefining C-suite accountability from tactical task proximity to intentional decision-boundary design as mandated by ISO/IEC 38500. Fusing deterministic technical controls with executive accountability allows organizations to safely scale autonomous systems without forfeiting enterprise governance integrity.

detail.abstract: Critical telecommunications infrastructure increasingly supports applications whose failure or delay can have consequences beyond ordinary user inconvenience, including industrial control, intelligent transportation, emergency response, and remote monitoring. Ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) therefore requires resource management that jointly considers delay, reliability, availability, interference, energy use, and service isolation. Conventional optimization remains valuable because it can encode explicit constraints, but dynamic network conditions and large action spaces can make repeated optimization computationally expensive. Machine learning (ML), especially supervised prediction, deep reinforcement learning (DRL), and federated learning, offers ways to anticipate demand and adapt resource allocation to changing conditions. This paper reviews research on ML-based radio resource management, network slicing, cloud radio access networks, and URLLC, and develops a conceptual framework for critical telecom infrastructure. The review emphasizes that learning-based policies should not be treated as inherently reliable: performance depends on representative training data, suitable reward design, generalization under distribution shift, and safe integration with network control. A layered framework is proposed in which telemetry supports prediction, a constrained decision policy allocates radio and computing resources, a safety gate checks service-level requirements, and network measurements close the feedback loop. The framework is a literature-grounded synthesis, not a tested implementation. The paper identifies research needs in tail-latency evaluation, reliability-aware learning, multi-slice coordination, explainability, security, and deployment validation. It argues that hybrid ML-and-optimization architectures, with deterministic fallback and operational oversight, provide a more credible path toward dependable resource management than unconstrained autonomous learning alone.

detail.abstract: When large language models from different companies screen the same job applications, they tend to reject the same people. We ask what these screeners share, whether it drives their decisions, and why. Seven LLM screeners from four vendors judged 800 synthetic resumes, each paired with a job description, and four of them also judged 800 real loan applications with known repayment. For each screener we estimate its template: the decision rule, not a resume layout, that links measurable features of the text to its decisions. Three findings emerge. First, all seven share one template on resumes, and its strongest ingredient is the job description's own vocabulary. Second, that ingredient is causal. Rewriting a resume to use the job description's exact terms, without changing its facts, turns rejections into selections ten times as often as the reverse. Synonyms and reformatting have no measurable effect. The LLM we used for the rewriting, told not to fabricate, added unsupported claims to 16 of the 25 rewrites that flipped a decision, and the screeners rewarded those most. Third, the template applies when there is a job description to match. On loan narratives, which have none, text features explain little of any screener's decisions, and the screeners approve between 42% and 86% of the same loans while none predicts repayment better than chance. A simple model explains the shared rule: a screener credits each requirement it recognizes, by meaning or by exact words, whichever is stronger. The model also predicts, and the data confirm, that a faithful keyword rewrite tips only resumes already close to the bar. The vendors' own technical reports show the training steps that could make that weighting common to all of them. We release a calibrated audit that needs no demographic data.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted independently using publicly available data from the 2021 American Time Use Survey (ATUS) and its Well-Being Module, provided by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

detail.abstract: Background: Working from home has become an important feature of contemporary employment, yet evidence regarding its relationship with worker well-being remains mixed. Examining individual dimensions of experienced well-being may identify associations that are obscured when well-being is treated as a single overall construct. Methods: This study used the 2021 American Time Use Survey (ATUS) Well-Being Module to examine differences in experienced well-being between work performed at home and work performed at the respondent's workplace. The analytic sample included 1,254 work activities contributed by 1,069 respondents, including 486 home and 768 workplace activities. Six activitylevel outcomes were examined on 0-6 scales: happiness, meaning, stress, tiredness, sadness, and pain. Weighted linear regression models adjusted for demographic and employment characteristics. Sampling variance was estimated using the 160 Bureau of Labor Statistics Well-Being Activity Replicate Weights, and Holm-adjusted p-values accounted for testing six primary outcomes. Results: After adjustment, work performed at home was associated with lower experienced pain compared with work performed at the workplace (β =-0.328, SE = 0.119, 95% CI [-0.561,-0.095], p = .006). The association remained statistically significant after Holm correction for multiple testing (adjusted p = .035). No statistically significant adjusted differences were observed for happiness, meaning, stress, tiredness, or sadness. The pain association remained negative in sensitivity analyses that omitted usual weekly work hours (β =-0.298) and added weekly earnings (β =-0.278). Conclusions: Work performed at home was associated with lower experienced pain, but not with statistically significant differences in the other five dimensions of experienced well-being examined. The findings suggest that associations between work location and well-being may be dimensionspecific rather than uniformly positive or negative. Because the analysis is observational, the results should not be interpreted as evidence that working from home causes lower pain.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming organizational decision-making through data analysis, automation, predictive modeling, and intelligent optimization. However, sustainable benefits depend on more than technological capability; they also require reliable information, employee participation, accountability, effective governance, and enterprise risk management. Fragmented digital transformation initiatives may create operational inefficiencies, unreliable decisions, and governance failures that undermine long-term performance. This article develops a conceptual framework integrating AI-enabled decision-making, systems thinking, and risk governance to explain how organizations can achieve sustainable performance through trustworthy digital decisions. Drawing on systems theory, organizational learning, dynamic capabilities, AI governance, enterprise risk management, and digital financial reporting, the study identifies four interconnected dimensions: digital capability, systems-oriented organizational learning, riskaware governance, and responsible decision implementation. The framework proposes that AI generates sustainable organizational value when its outputs rely on reliable data, reflect operational contexts, align with strategic objectives, and receive appropriate oversight. It also examines how feedback mechanisms connect technological performance, managerial decisions, organizational learning, and risk controls. Eight conceptual propositions address the potential roles of data quality, system reliability, governance maturity, employee participation, and crossfunctional coordination. The study contributes to management theory by integrating technological, organizational, and governance perspectives into a unified framework for trustworthy digital decision-making. Practical implications include clarifying decision ownership, implementing proportionate risk controls, maintaining traceable information flows, and evaluating operational, financial, and organizational outcomes. As a conceptual study, it provides a foundation for future quantitative, qualitative, and longitudinal research into responsible innovation, organizational resilience, and sustainable business performance.

detail.abstract: This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled predictive analytics, telematics, and intelligent decision support may improve fleet optimization and operational resilience in U.S. car rental operations. It proposes a structured literaturebased review and thematic synthesis of research on predictive maintenance, connectedvehicle technologies, demand forecasting, fleet allocation, and transportation resilience. The review is intended to identify how these capabilities may support vehicle availability, maintenance planning, resource allocation, and responses to operational disruptions. Building on literature concerning smart fleet management, AI-driven decision support, predictive maintenance, and sustainability analytics, the article develops an integrated conceptual framework linking operational data, AI analytics, managerial decisions, fleet actions, and resilience outcomes. The framework also considers the influence of data quality, system interoperability, organizational capability, cybersecurity, and human oversight on the translation of analytical insights into operational practice. Rather than assuming that AI adoption automatically improves performance, the article treats AI as a decision-support capability whose value depends on implementation conditions, managerial judgment, and appropriate governance. The proposed framework provides a foundation for understanding relationships among technological capabilities, operational decisions, and resilience in rental-fleet management. Its propositions require further empirical evaluation using operational data and comparative studies of U.S. car rental organizations.

title: Silent Shares: What If Shareholder Democracy Has Negative Value?

detail.abstract:
Corporate law assumes that shareholders value their votes, and the market for initial public offerings suggests they value them little: in 2025 issuers used a dual-class structure in two of every five offerings, the voting premium at American firms is a few percent, and the campaign against low-vote stock since 2017 has identified no injured buyer. The investment advisers who hold much of the vote cast nearly every ballot, though neither the Securities and Exchange Commission nor the Labor Department requires it. The puzzle is why.

One way to resolve the puzzle is to recognize that the shareholder vote is a club good, so its value is subject to congestion. Its value to each holder falls when ballots cast on purchased analysis count one recommendation many times and make it less likely that an informed ballot decides the outcome. An index fund manager keeps twelve basis points of any gain an informed vote produces, so on routine matters it casts the ballot a proxy adviser recommends.

I propose a safe harbor for a disclosed choice not to vote uncontested director elections, advisory votes on pay and precatory proposals, expressed in a proxy that withholds authority on them and counts toward the quorum; contested and fundamental votes stay inside the duty.

The paper responds to the Securities and Exchange Commission's proposal to rescind Rule 14a-8, which requires companies to put qualifying shareholder proposals on their proxy cards, and draws out implications for the Commission's temporary exemption under Section 36(a)(1), which lets tokenized NMS stock trade on distributed-ledger venues that need not perform the trading oversight a registered exchange must.

detail.abstract: The digitalization of halal certification represents an important component of the transformation of halal industry services and governance. However, the availability of a digital platform does not automatically ensure its acceptance or effective use by business actors. This article develops a conceptual framework for explaining the adoption of digital halal certification platforms through a synthesis of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework. A critical literature review approach is employed to compare foundational technology acceptance theories, organizational technology adoption research, digital transformation studies, and Indonesian halal assurance regulations. Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are examined as individual-level technology acceptance factors, while organizational readiness and regulatory support are considered internal and external conditions that may facilitate adoption. The synthesis produces four propositions concerning the expected positive relationships between these factors and platform adoption. The article contributes conceptually by connecting user acceptance with organizational capabilities and the institutional environment in a legally regulated certification context. It does not claim that the proposed model has been empirically validated or that previous studies have never integrated TAM and TOE in the halal sector. Further research is required to test the propositions while accounting for differences in business characteristics, digital literacy, certification schemes, and patterns of platform use.

detail.abstract: This thesis investigates whether the Project Management Office (PMO) can act as a strategic integrator to enhance cross-functional collaboration and decision-making among C-Level executives during restructuring in Swiss cantonal banks. The Credit Suisse collapse in 2023 and the subsequent rise in regulatory and public scrutiny illustrate how quickly executive alignment can weaken under transformation pressure, particularly in institutions operating under public mandates. The study brings together four literature streams that are often treated separately: decision-making processes, organizational resistance, collaborative mechanisms, and PMO positioning. This synthesis frames executive collaboration as a governance challenge that depends on coherent decision structures, clear roles, and practical coordination mechanisms. The empirical base consists of 24 semi-structured interviews with C-Level executives across four Swiss cantonal banks, covering six executive functions. The analysis follows a qualitative approach combining grounded theory and a functional cluster comparison in order to capture how restructuring generates different lived experiences across executive roles and how these differences influence collaboration. The findings converge into three insights. First, a PMO paradox emerges. The PMO is broadly recognized as essential for coordination, yet its effectiveness is contested, and perceived neutrality tends to matter more than formal mandate. Second, functional divergence is systematic. Collaboration levers differ across executive functions, which limits the relevance of standardized interventions. Third, context constrains decision mechanisms. In cantonal banks, hybrid decision approaches remain largely preparatory because the public mandate and Board oversight require centralized validation. Based on these patterns, the thesis proposes a Four-Layer Governance Integration Model. It suggests that PMO effectiveness depends on four enabling conditions operating at the same time: explicit CEO-backed executive positioning, a facilitation posture rather than control, structured coordination through shared references and governance rituals, and adaptive implementation aligned with functional realities.

title: Protective Settlements: How Corporations Pay to Shield Insiders from Liability
affiliations: Ono Academic College Faculty of Law

detail.title: Protective Settlements: How Corporations Pay to Shield Insiders from Liability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

affiliations.org_name: Ono Academic College - Faculty of Law

detail.abstract:
Corporate law knows how to police self-dealing. Once a conflict is visible, courts withdraw business judgment deference and apply loyalty-based tools to scrutinize the transaction. This Article identifies a category of conflicted transactions that escapes those tools: the protective settlement, a regulatory resolution in which a corporation uses its assets to shield a controller, director, or officer from credible personal liability. Negotiated under enforcement pressure, obscured by confidentiality, and bundled into a broader corporate resolution, the insider benefit typically escapes detection and therefore evades review as a conflicted transaction.

The 2019 Facebook-FTC settlement provides a rare window into the mechanics of these bargains. Reconstructing the negotiations from a fragmented public record, this Article shows that Facebook first offered $1 billion, then $3 billion on the condition that the FTC drop its demand to name Mark Zuckerberg personally, and finally agreed to $5 billion once his protection was assured. This sequence suggests that Zuckerberg’s release carried independent economic value, paid for with corporate assets. Shareholders financed both Facebook’s regulatory peace and protection for its CEO. From this case, the Article derives four markers of insider protection and applies them to some of the largest enforcement resolutions of the past fifteen years. One or more markers appear in settlements involving Amazon, Boeing, BP, HSBC, Goldman Sachs, and BNP Paribas. Corporations may have legitimate reasons to resolve insider exposure, but no corporate law mechanism reliably tests whether the protection was purchased on terms consistent with shareholder interests.

The Article’s central claim is that protective settlements are conflicted transactions and should be reviewed as such. In Maffei v. Palkon, the Delaware Supreme Court applied business judgment review to a liability-reducing reincorporation undertaken on a “clear day,” but expressly reserved transactions that protect insiders from existing exposure arising out of past conduct. Protective settlements occupy that reserved category, and no Delaware decision has yet supplied a standard for reviewing them. Moreover, existing doctrine is poorly suited for the task, as entire fairness asks courts to assess a fair price for a benefit with no market comparator; post-SB 21 cleansing may restore deference precisely when scrutiny is most needed; and corporate waste captures only the most extreme cases.

The Article’s proposed loyalty-centered framework surfaces protective settlements through regulatory statements and dissents, enhanced Section 220 inspection, and mandatory disclosure of insider releases. It then asks courts to treat a credibly pleaded protective settlement as presumptively wasteful, rebuttable only through a process-oriented good-faith inquiry modeled on Zapata Corp. v. Maldonado. When the presumption stands, the protected insider should bear the protective premium. If Delaware law aggressively monitors insiders when they extract value through mergers, compensation, and controller transactions, it should not go silent when they extract value through settlement.

detail.abstract: The paper examines the impact of US QE on the financial conditions of the “Fragile Five” emerging market economies before and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Using panel data from January 2012 to September 2023, we analyse the transmission channels of US QE through portfolio flows, equity returns, and exchange rates. Our findings reveal significant differences between pre-COVID and post COVID periods. While QE3 primarily influenced equity returns indirectly through portfolio flows, post COVID QE had a more direct and pronounced effect on both equity returns and exchange rates. The study highlights the importance of domestic macroeconomic conditions in moderating QE’s impact, with countries like India and Indonesia benefitting more due to stable economic fundamentals. Conversely, countries with high inflation and external debt, such as Turkey, experienced muted effects. The research underscores the heterogeneous responses among the Fragile Five and emphasizes the role of global financial uncertainty in shaping QE’s effectiveness.

title: Who Manufactured Pseudo-history Theories? The Emergent Collective Creation of Historical Narratives on the Chinese Internet

detail.title: Who Manufactured Pseudo-history Theories? The Emergent Collective Creation of Historical Narratives on the Chinese Internet

detail.abstract: This paper examines the formation, expansion, and functions of pseudo-history theories (伪史论) on the Chinese internet from the perspective of cultural economics, and proposes the analytical concept of “Emergent Collective Creation.” This concept refers to the process whereby a large number of relatively independent content producers, acting on the basis of their respective local motivations and in the absence of any unified overall plan, generate a collective narrative system that exceeds the original planning and control of any single participant through imitation, competition, the recombination of arguments, and the migration of topics. The paper first investigates relevant figures who possess formal academic credentials or publishing experience and analyzes the pathways through which early pseudo-history resources entered public circulation. It then takes as examples the extension of pseudo-history theories from ancient Greece and Rome to other civilizations, historical figures, and issues concerning Chinese dynastic history, exploring how competition for traffic, content imitation, and the selective recombination of historical materials drive narrative expansion. Finally, using online controversies surrounding the film The Penghu Naval Battle as a case study, it analyzes how pseudo-history theories have been deployed by different participants in conflicts over historical identity and in online opinion confrontation, and discusses possible links between controversial historical discourses and public trust in academic authority. The paper argues that even dispersed individual actions lacking unified coordination may, through indirect interaction, produce collective narrative outcomes and enable pseudo-history theories to move from a form of content competition for traffic into ideological contention. Because this study relies primarily on publicly available online materials, publications, and media reports, and lacks internal platform data as well as continuous records at the creator level, the mechanisms identified remain exploratory explanations whose chains of transmission, causal relations, and actual effects await further verification.

detail.abstract: Background: This study aims to determine the factors that influence consumer behavior toward Online Food Delivery Services (OFDS) in Bangladesh. Objectives: The data used in this study were collected through an online survey. Methodology: A range of quantitative techniques were adopted to collect data from the target groups, where a sample of Bangladeshi consumers (n=300) was used to consider the measurement and structural models by applying a Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) method. This study used repeat purchase intention as a proxy for customer satisfaction. This study estimated the relationship between repeat purchase intentions and seven latent variables. Results: The study's findings show that refund policy perception has the strongest impact on repeat purchase intention, followed by perceived convenience, condition of food delivered, perceived friendliness of delivery person, and time-saving perception, although perceived product information and transaction security are not significant. Using survey data from urban OFDS users in Bangladesh, the findings reflect consumer decision-making in a post-pandemic stabilized platform environment. Conclusion: The results further indicate that certain hygiene factors such as transaction security and basic product information no longer differentiate repeat purchase intentions, highlighting a shift from adoption-driven to experience-driven consumption logic in mature digital service markets.

detail.abstract:
Article 22(1) of Canada’s 2021 Model Foreign Investment Promotion and Protection Agreement provides that the agreement does not prevent Canada from adopting or maintaining a measure “necessary to fulfill” Aboriginal or treaty rights recognized and affirmed by section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982. No tribunal has yet interpreted the clause. The word “necessary” assumes a fixed obligation against which a measure can be tested. The duty to consult provides none, because it is a graduated standard whose content varies with the strength of the claim and the seriousness of the impact. Deciding whether a measure was necessary to fulfil section 35 therefore requires deciding what section 35 required. Article 32(3) of the Model withholds that question from tribunals and directs them to the prevailing interpretation of Canadian courts.

The paper traces the clause’s lineage from New Zealand’s Treaty of Waitangi exception through CPTPP article 29.6 and CUSMA article 32.5. It shows that the Model drops three safeguards those provisions contain: self-judging language, a chapeau, and a carve-out for the interpretation of domestic obligations. Drawing on the Model’s text, the Bilcon and Windstream arbitrations, and the limits of annulment and set-aside, it argues that “necessary” should require only good faith and a rational connection to an identified section 35 obligation, not least-restrictive means. It also shows that affected Indigenous peoples have no guaranteed role in the proceedings that would construe their rights. The paper closes with implications for energy investors and Crown counsel, and with three drafting reforms to the Model.

title: The Impact of Sustainability Reporting on Directors' ESG Duties: The Disclosure-Duty Feedback Loop
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Faculty of Law

detail.title: The Impact of Sustainability Reporting on Directors' ESG Duties: The Disclosure-Duty Feedback Loop

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 970/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Law Working Paper Series

affiliations.org_name: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Faculty of Law

detail.abstract:
Maturation of sustainability reporting has expanded, rather than resolved, the ambiguity surrounding directors’ ESG duties. Reporting standards specify what must be disclosed, but not what directors must do behind the disclosure, while regulatory regimes diverge in scope, materiality and enforcement. The paper explains this paradox through a “disclosure-duty feedback loop”. Because company law regulates process rather than outcomes, mandatory reporting requires boards to establish and oversee systems capable of producing reliable disclosures, drawing them into the governance of the underlying subject matter. Each report then becomes a benchmark against which subsequent board conduct may be assessed, causing the obligation to ratchet upward as disclosure becomes mandatory and assured.

The paper traces this loop across three regimes: an ISSB baseline adopted in Singapore and the United Kingdom; an EU regime narrowed by Omnibus I but retaining a commitment to double materiality; and a US regime withdrawn at the federal level, while California extends reporting obligations extraterritorially. It shows that the loop operates through existing duties, with three channels in the United Kingdom, two in Singapore and effectively one in Delaware. The loop therefore inherits the limits of those duties in standard, foreseeability and enforcement, and is strained where listing and incorporation jurisdictions diverge. It strengthens monitoring without making directors guarantors of ESG outcomes. The paper proposes four reforms: clearer oversight duties, safe harbours for good-faith forward-looking and Scope 3 disclosures, proportionate assurance, and mutual recognition for dual reporters.
