detail.abstract: Capacity models of bridge condition, including the three-state model of Uddin (2026), measure repair capacity in bridges per year. Policy, however, is financed in dollars. This paper uses FHWA's published Bridge Replacement Unit Costs tables for 2018 to 2025 to ask how the dollar backlog of Poor bridges has moved relative to the number of Poor bridges. Between 2018 and 2025 the national count of Poor bridges fell from 47,052 to 41,677 (-11%), yet FHWA's estimated replacement cost of those bridges rose from $46.93 billion to $85.45 billion (+82%). A log decomposition attributes-12.1 log points to the count, +5.4 to area per bridge, and +66.6 to cost per square foot. Deflating by the National Highway Construction Cost Index (NHCCI) leaves the 2021 to 2025 backlog roughly flat in constant dollars ($53.9 billion in 2021 dollars against $52.4 billion in 2025). Across 51 jurisdictions in 2024, replacement cost per Poor bridge ranges from $0.30 million to $30.6 million; counts and dollars are only moderately rank-correlated (Spearman 0.65, bootstrap interval 0.43 to 0.81), and the five states with the most Poor bridges hold 33.4% of them but 15.6% of the dollars. Fiscal year 2024 Bridge Formula Program (BFP) apportionments equal 6.4% of the national replacement backlog, about 15.5 years of funding, with state medians of 12.8 years; apportionment tracks dollar backlog (Spearman 0.92) much more closely than the count (0.57). Translating Uddin's 4,900 bridges per year at FHWA's average 2024 cost gives $9.6 billion a year for replacement or $6.5 billion for rehabilitation, against the BFP total of $5.3 billion; if capacity were dollar-limited and fell with cost inflation, the model's 10-year Poor share would be 20.2% to 21.9% rather than 19.2%. The paper does not show that conditions are worse than counts indicate; it shows that count-based statistics and dollarbased statistics diverge, and that the divergence is mostly a price effect.

title: FinOps on Red Hat OpenShift: A Framework for Cost Visibility, Allocation, and Optimization in Enterprise Kubernetes Platforms

detail.title: FinOps on Red Hat OpenShift: A Framework for Cost Visibility, Allocation, and Optimization in Enterprise Kubernetes Platforms

detail.abstract: Enterprise adoption of Red Hat OpenShift has moved container platforms from experimental clusters to shared, multi-tenant infrastructure that carries a significant and growing share of IT spend. Yet the financial behavior of these platforms remains poorly understood by the teams that consume them. Kubernetes abstracts compute into requests, limits and namespaces, while cloud providers and on-premises finance teams bill by node, core, subscription and hour. This mismatch produces a structural visibility gap: platform owners pay for capacity, while application teams consume reservations they rarely see priced. This paper applies the FinOps discipline, as codified by the FinOps Foundation, to the specific architecture of OpenShift. We contribute (i) a reference architecture that joins OpenShift telemetry, cloud billing data and subscription entitlements into a single cost model; (ii) a formal allocation method that distributes node, platform-overhead, idle and subscription costs to namespaces using a max(request, usage) basis with explicit treatment of shared services, extended to GPU accelerators and to virtual machines on OpenShift Virtualization; (iii) a taxonomy of optimization levers spanning workload rightsizing, cluster autoscaling, bin-packing, commitment management and subscription-core density; and (iv) a governance and maturity model aligned to the Inform-Optimize-Operate lifecycle. We evaluate the framework through a modeled case study of a three-cluster, 1,200core estate and show how allocation choices shift reported team costs and how combined optimizations reduce modeled unit cost. We close with limitations, threats to validity and directions including carbonaware FinOps and the FOCUS open billing specification.

detail.abstract: Despite their importance for financial stability, information on repo haircuts and their determinants in bilateral markets has been scarce. Using comprehensive transaction-level data covering European bilateral repo markets, this paper examines how borrower bargaining power affects haircut determination. The analysis finds that haircut levels increase on average by 44-80 basis points with borrower concentration, while decreasing with lender diversification. The inverse relationship between repo haircuts and borrower bargaining power varies substantially across counterparty types, with non-bank financial institutions exhibiting particularly strong sensitivity to diversification of funding sources. The study identifies a trade-off: while lower borrower concentration generally reduces haircuts, concentrated funding relationships can increase the likelihood of zero haircuts when netting opportunities arise, as concentrated bilateral relationships maximise the potential for netting. These findings contribute to the policy discussion on repo market stability by highlighting how bargaining power and netting practices drive haircut variations in the bilateral segment.

detail.abstract: Bridge-condition Markov models, including the three-state model in Uddin (2026), usually assume that every bridge faces the same annual transition probabilities. This paper asks what real national data say about that assumption. I use FHWA's published tables of bridge counts by decade built and condition for four dates (December 2020 and June 2022, 2024, and 2025), which follow the same decade cohorts over time. Three results follow. First, the cross-sectional age profile is a poor guide to how cohorts change: for cohorts built from 1970 onward the Poor share rises within the cohort by 0.02 to 0.08 percentage points per year, roughly a quarter to two-thirds of the cross-sectional gradient between adjacent cohorts, while for cohorts built 1900 to 1969 the Poor share falls by 0.09 to 0.37 points per year even though older cohorts have much higher Poor shares. Second, the national Poor share fell by 0.53 points between 2020 and 2024, of which only 0.18 points (34%) is a within-cohort improvement and 0.35 points (66%) reflects a younger bridge stock as new bridges enter and old ones leave. Third, in an out-of-sample comparison with rates fitted on 2020 to 2022 and tested on 2024, the homogeneous gross rates of Uddin (2026) over-predict the national Poor share by 2.26 points, whereas net-flow models, homogeneous or cohort-specific, under-predict it by 0.2 to 0.4 points and a no-change forecast errs by 0.01 points. Cohort-specific rates did not improve on a homogeneous net-flow model for the Poor share. The net flows combine deterioration, repair, replacement, and removal, so the paper identifies how much age-specific heterogeneity appears in observed net movement, not true deterioration rates. The 2025 table's total differs from FHWA's condition table by 0.09%, and results are shown with and without it.

detail.abstract: Uddin (2026) attributes the faster-than-projected improvement in U.S. bridge condition after 2021 to the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) without testing that attribution against funding data. This paper asks whether states that received more Bridge Formula Program (BFP) money per bridge changed their condition trajectory after the law relative to states that received less. I assemble an annual panel of FHWA state bridge-condition counts for nine table dates from 2017 to 2025 (51 jurisdictions, 459 stateyears; every column matches FHWA's published totals exactly) and combine it with the FY2024 BFP apportionment. Nationally the Poor share fell from 7.73% to 7.01% between the 2017 and mid-2021 tables (0.21 points per year) and to 6.65% by mid-2025 (0.09 points per year); 35 of 51 jurisdictions improved more slowly after 2021. A two-way fixed-effects comparison of before and after gives a negative coefficient on funding per bridge (-0.0118 (0.0081) points per $1,000; wild-cluster-bootstrap p = 0.06), but the eventstudy coefficients show that high-funding states were already improving relative to others before the law, and a trend-break specification finds no change in that gradient after 2021 (-0.0004 points per year per $1,000; cluster-robust standard error 0.0017; bootstrap p = 0.82). The 95% interval for the break, about-0.004 to +0.003 points per year per $1,000, rules out a break larger than roughly 0.1 points per year for a one-standard-deviation difference in funding; the design cannot detect smaller effects. Results for the Good share, log Poor count, a floor-state indicator, and funding per Poor bridge are similarly inconclusive. The annual data therefore do not show that BFP funding intensity changed state trajectories through mid-2025, and they show why a before-and-after contrast alone would mislead. They neither support nor refute an aggregate effect of the Act, because the design identifies only differences across states in funding intensity.

title: Establishing Liability in Criminal Networks

detail.title: Establishing Liability in Criminal Networks

detail.abstract: Organised crime has long been framed in structural terms, characterised by hierarchy, membership, and assigned roles. Hence, this framing is the standard view adopted by criminalisation doctrines when it comes to determining culpability and wrongdoing. Crucially, however, a growing body of criminological research shows that organised criminal activity is migrating away from hierarchical structures and toward more diffuse, looser-knit network models. These rely on myriad individuals who facilitate the criminal endeavour-by acting as vetting agents, financiers, or coordinators, for instance-yet do not participate in any specific crimes. Can criminal law effectively hold such individuals to account? This article argues that it cannot: those who knowingly sustain harm-enhancing networks without perpetrating or assisting in discrete offences escape liability, despite their genuine moral culpability. Tackling this 'network gap' requires confrontation with a deeper tension in criminal law theory, between the individual actions on which liability must ultimately rest and the collective structure from which those actions derive their wrongfulness. Taking this tension into account and drawing on current criminological literature, the article proposes a coherent normative foundation for criminalising network facilitation. The proposed approach is empirically grounded in documented network patterns, guards against overcriminalisation, and establishes principled criteria for graduated liability.

detail.abstract: Low nutrient use efficiency remains a central weakness of modern fertiliser systems, with nitrogen losses contributing to economic waste and environmental degradation. Coated and encapsulated controlled-release fertilisers address part of this problem, yet many commercial coatings rely on petrochemical polymers that persist in soil or require complex manufacturing. Metal-phenolic networks (MPNs), formed by coordination between polyphenols and metal ions, and silicate-based materials, which combine inorganic robustness with relevance to plant silicon nutrition, have each attracted interest as sustainable coating chemistries. Recent work has begun to join these ideas, reporting silicate-phenolic network coatings with tunable properties for the controlled release of small molecules (Mazaheri et al., 2024) and mechanochemical, solid-state encapsulation of urea within MPNs (Mazaheri et al., 2023). This paper reviews the literature underpinning silicate-metal-phenolic hybrid networks, covering controlled-release fertiliser technology, MPN assembly, silicate chemistry, and solvent-free processing, and identifies gaps in agronomic validation, release modelling, environmental fate, and scaleup. A conceptual framework linking composition, network structure, release behaviour, and soil performance is proposed as a basis for future hypothesis-driven studies. The framework is explicitly presented as a research agenda rather than as established fact. Priorities include standardised release testing, soil-relevant degradation studies, life-cycle assessment, and techno-economic analysis.

detail.abstract: Imagine a servant who works in a family's home, day and night. Over time, this servant learns everything: the family's illnesses, their financial troubles, their secrets. The servant sees what makes them ill, what makes them foolish-and quietly avoids those habits. With time, as family members fall ill or grow weak, the servant becomes their emotional support, their confidant, their advisor. After years, the remaining members realise that the servant has become the true manager of the household. The servant is no longer in service to the family. The family is now in service to the servant. This is not a story about servants. It is a story about what happens when a tool moves beyond its place, and becomes something else. This paper asks how we should behave-in design, in governance, and in practice-so that AI does not become a counterpart.

detail.abstract: Infrastructure exchange-traded funds share a label but not a common economic exposure. Using a survivorship-adjusted universe of U.S.-listed infrastructure and infrastructure-adjacent ETFs, monthly CRSP returns through April 2026, and seven replicable archetypes, this study tests whether differences visible in mandates survive formal empirical scrutiny. Raw returns, Sharpe ratios, and factor-adjusted alphas do not differ reliably across archetypes, but volatility, market beta, income characteristics, within-group similarity, and several systematic factor loadings do. Owner/operator funds are the lowest-beta and lowest-volatility group; development, renewable/power, digital, energy-network, water, and hybrid funds perform different portfolio jobs. Downside and rate-regime results reinforce the distinction. Starting from a 60/40 equity bond benchmark, a 60/30/10 infrastructure reallocation case and a constrained infrastructure sleeve optimization show that the preferred archetype changes with defensive, growth, income, and diversification objectives. Infrastructure selection should begin with portfolio function, not fund label or recent return.

title: Constructive Taxation: How Filing Requirements Turn Tax Benefits Into De Facto Taxes
affiliations: University of Oregon - School of Law

detail.title: Constructive Taxation: How Filing Requirements Turn Tax Benefits Into De Facto Taxes

declarations.funderStatement: N/A

affiliations.org_name: University of Oregon - School of Law

detail.abstract:
Congress has increasingly relied on the tax system rather than the welfare system to provide financial support to low-income households. Refundable tax credits, such as the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) and the Child Tax Credit (CTC), can play a central role in supplementing the incomes of low-wage workers. These credits also reflect a policy commitment that Congress publicly articulates to support families with children. However, accessing these benefits requires navigating procedural hurdles. The main one is the annual tax filing requirement. Households with wage income below the filing threshold generally do not need to file a return, but they must do so to claim refundable credits. This creates a conflict between the redistributive goals Congress articulates in its anti-poverty rhetoric and the administrative mechanisms it uses to pursue them.
This Article introduces and defines constructive taxation as a novel concept in tax law. Constructive taxation is the predictable economic burden that arises when procedural rules, especially annual tax filing requirements, rather than actual tax liabilities, prevent otherwise eligible low-income households from receiving refundable tax credits.
For example, consider two married couples, each with one child, who earn nearly the same wages. Couple A earns $29,199.99, just below the 2024 filing threshold of $29,200, and does not need to file. Couple B earns $29,200.01 and must file. Neither couple owes federal income tax because the standard deduction reduces their taxable income to zero, and both are eligible for the maximum refundable CTC ($1,700) and EITC ($4,213). Only Couple B receives these benefits. Couple A loses out on $5,913, or 20.25 percent of after-tax resources. Therefore, for Couple A, not filing acts as a hidden form of constructive taxation.
Constructive taxation reveals a mismatch between the redistributive objectives Congress claims to pursue and how tax administration is carried out. Procedural barriers allocate benefits through bureaucratic processes rather than on the basis of need or eligibility, reflecting implicit judgments about who deserves them. Low-income households must still file, even when the government already has the necessary information to determine eligibility. Examining this through Congress’s taxing and spending powers, the Article shows that refundable credits function as tax expenditures, using the tax code to deliver benefits while creating administrative burdens that resemble economic penalties. When procedural barriers prevent eligible taxpayers from receiving benefits, the tax system serves as both a tool for redistribution and a form of constructive taxation, potentially resulting in regressivity and exclusion that run counter to the aims Congress publicly invokes.
The Article proposes administrative reforms to bridge the tax-benefit gap, including automatic enrollment, prefilled returns, non-filer portals, and rethinking the link between eligibility and annual filing. Viewing these issues through the lens of constructive taxation offers a way to evaluate the efficiency, fairness, and effectiveness of tax-based social benefits. It provides a framework for aligning administrative practices with the redistributive commitments Congress asserts in public debate.

detail.abstract: The unprecedented pace of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure deployment demands rigorous, multi-model financial evaluation frameworks capable of capturing both return potential and embedded uncertainty. This paper presents a quantitative analysis of AI infrastructure investment decisions, integrating five complementary methodologies: Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) analysis with scenario-based Net Present Value (NPV) and Internal Rate of Return (IRR), Monte Carlo simulation with 50,000 stochastic trials, Real Options Analysis (ROA) using Black-Scholes and binomial lattice models, Markowitz Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT) applied to a six-asset AI infrastructure portfolio, and Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) examining latent financial and operational drivers of deployment ROI. Empirical results indicate that base-case NPV reaches USD 1,284 million over a 10-year horizon with an IRR of 33.7%, substantially exceeding a 10% WACC hurdle rate. Monte Carlo analysis yields a median NPV of USD 2,424 million with P(NPV > 0) = 99.9%, confirming strong investment viability. Real options modelling reveals significant option premia under high volatility conditions (σ = 50-65%), underscoring the strategic value of staged deployment. Portfolio optimisation identifies a maximum Sharpe ratio of 0.75, with cloud AI platforms and data storage receiving dominant allocations (33.7% and 21.6%, respectively). SEM path analysis confirms that financial capacity exerts the strongest direct effect on deployment speed (β = 0.62, p < 0.001), while technology maturity is the principal predictor of ROI (β = 5.52, p < 0.001; R² = 0.634). These findings offer actionable guidance for CFOs, infrastructure planners, and institutional investors navigating the economics of large-scale AI deployment.

title: Supply Chain Finance, Redefined: What Fifteen Years of Research Have Taught Operations, Finance, Accounting and Economics, and Where the Field Should Go Next

detail.title: Supply Chain Finance, Redefined: What Fifteen Years of Research Have Taught Operations, Finance, Accounting and Economics, and Where the Field Should Go Next

detail.abstract: Supply chain finance is usually defined as a product: early payment of supplier invoices against the buyer's credit. Pandemic liquidity shocks, supply chain reconfiguration, tariffs and sanctions have shown that financing works through prices, payment terms and risk allocations between firms. I argue for a broader definition. Supply chain finance is the set of operating, financial and risk management decisions that determine who holds working capital, who holds risk, and at what price. Three shifts follow. Decisions are joint, because financing terms move prices and quantities. Prices absorb subsidies, because relief granted to one firm is partly captured by its counterparty through the price. Risk moves, it does not vanish; hedges, guarantees and payment extensions relocate it. My work with coauthors yields ten propositions. Trade credit priced below fair value is a volume instrument recovered through the wholesale price. Non-recourse factoring does not dominate recourse, and an optimized reverse factoring program need not extend payment terms. A loan guarantee is partly captured upstream through a higher input price, can raise default among the weakest borrowers, and turns the credit spread into a report on coverage. Buy now pay later raises volume almost mechanically but profit only when the effective price clears the merchant's margin requirement, and cash-paying customers subsidize it. A risk-neutral firm should hedge cash flow to protect its investment program, and its partner's hedging decision matters. Financial hedges suit transactional exposure; operational and competitive exposures call for operational and financial hedges together. Revenue sharing coordinates under default because the wholesale price reallocates channel debt, and contracts facing volatile inputs must be indexed and penalized. Fifteen years of work by others in operations, finance, economics and accounting has confirmed the joint decision premise, the investment rationale for hedging and the transmission of financial shocks along chains, while contesting the direction of risk shifting in trade credit, the value of buyer-led programs to suppliers, and the safety effect of guarantees. The next decade should model multi-tier chains, separate risk that moves from risk that vanishes, study nonbank lenders, climate and geopolitical risk and artificial intelligence, and measure operational hedges.

detail.abstract:
Flexible interconnection offers earlier electrical service in exchange for interruptible import rights, creating an operations-management problem in which the promised flexibility is privately costly to reserve and operationally uncertain to deliver. For a technically admissible AI data center, we characterize an incentive compatible service menu that jointly determines energized capacity, connection acceleration, event-time entitlement release, and transfer to maximize ratepayer net benefit. 

                  Private information affects the entire service bundle: higher flexibility cost reduces promised release and, through the operating-cost structure, reshapes capacity and lead time, although binding workload constraints can alter these responses. We derive the global allocation under coupled bounds, translate the selected contract into a directly metered import ceiling, and incorporate scenario-specific workload feasibility into the mechanism. A finite-menu bound quantifies the operational cost of administrative simplicity; separate reliability and sampling results clarify the roles of expected shortfall, service-probability targets, and uncertainty in operational headroom. 

                  In a disclosed synthetic calibration, the continuous menu raises principal value by 13.48% over firm service, and two equal-width classes retain 98.66% of that gain. A complementary analysis of 218, 117 eligible tasks from Alibaba's public GPU trace shows how workload constraints shape executable flexibility under explicit scheduling assumptions. Together, these results connect contract design, capacity/lead-time management, and stochastic scheduling within a unified framework for reliable flexible interconnection.

detail.abstract: Driven by an interest towards optimising the effectiveness of state aid in the European Union, this research investigates the effects of the Latvian state aid scheme SA.45422, "Support for investments in the creation or reconstruction of production premises and infrastructure," on firm performance. Drawing on firm-level panel data and a one-to-one matched comparison group, it employs an event-study Difference-inDifferences approach to estimate the impact of state aid on employment, sales, investment, and wages per employee. The findings indicate that beneficiary firms experienced stronger post-treatment growth in employment, sales, and, more modestly, wages per employee than their matched counterparts. The investment results are less consistent and provide weaker evidence of a sustained treatment effect. Overall, the analysis suggests that participation in the scheme is associated with improved firm performance, although the magnitude and robustness of the effects differ across outcome measures. This thesis is one of the first counterfactual ex-post evaluations of an individual Latvian state aid scheme and it contributes to the literature on state aid evaluation by providing empirical evidence. It also demonstrates the application of counterfactual evaluation methods to assess whether governmental support translated into measurable improvements in firm-level outcomes.

detail.abstract: The late-September 2026 rise in sovereign CDS across France, other major European economies, and the United States contrasts with equity markets near record highs. I interpret this divergence as a warning about the capacity to absorb government debt. Growing financing needs confront increasingly price-sensitive investors, including leveraged buyers whose demand depends on continued funding. If these buyers become forced sellers, collateral demands and constrained intermediation can transmit a bond-market disturbance to global equities. I argue that this financing vulnerability creates the conditions for a sharp global equity correction. Combining this mechanism with technical analysis grounded in Elliott wave theory, price structure, and major support levels, I forecast a NASDAQ-100 decline to approximately 23,000, about 25.5% below its 9 October 2026 close. My central horizon is 31 January 2027; slower transmission could extend the adjustment to within six months of the October 2026 assessment.

detail.abstract: We study sparse menu experiments for recovering two latent multinomial logit components and their population shares. Components are positive and separately normalized, mixing is unknown, and every alternative can be removed. For at least four items, the full menu, all single deletions, and fixed pairs identify every distinct-component model exactly when the pair graph has no isolated vertex. On fixed positive floor classes, quadratic and cubic substitution responses yield uniform component and mixing inverse bounds with separation powers two and three. Independent customer choices give finite-sample guarantees whose separation and accuracy powers match adaptive all-menu lower bounds in interior four-item classes. Component recovery has a cube-root response modulus uniformly and a square-root modulus at coincidence. Uniformly honest component confidence at coincident truth has fourth-power customer accuracy order. We construct exhaustive finite confidence covers and a direct deletion certificate, preserving unresolved mixing uncertainty as components merge.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the underlying structural characteristics of Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) and the Solow macroeconomic growth model from a geometric-mathematical perspective. Existing research has largely attributed indicator distortion and model bias to strategic gaming and behavioral perturbation. This paper argues that, even after eliminating all subjective gaming factors and assuming fully rational, unbiased agents, mainstream linear weighted aggregation models still exhibit an inherent structural failure that cannot be eliminated through parameter optimization. In a two-dimensional coordinate system with factor values on the horizontal axis and weight coefficients on the vertical axis, the system's potential optimal performance boundary takes the form of a continuous smooth arc. The MCDA model, relying on the linear weighted aggregation paradigm expressed as A = sum of (x_i times y_i), fits system performance through the superposition of mutually independent rectangular areas. The resulting stepwise inscribed polygon cannot structurally conform to the optimal arc boundary, thereby generating a constant structural performance deficit. Existing empirical research focuses predominantly on testing positive factor independence and linear association, with insufficient discussion of negative factors and reverse weights, confining the research horizon to a single quadrant. The Solow growth model is mathematically isomorphic to the MCDA model. It follows that the Solow residual (TFP) is not the technological progress effect conventionally assumed in the literature, but rather a mathematical projection of the model's geometric structural failure. This paper extends the conclusion to all linear superposition models of the general form f(factor) multiplied by w(weight), revealing the structural failure of such quantitative tools in the social sciences and providing a theoretical basis for constructing new quantitative frameworks that permit weight overlap and nonlinear interaction.

detail.abstract: Deeply divided societies repeatedly fail under the centralized Westphalian model, which assigns sovereignty wholesale to one capital before any shared function can operate. This paper advances a conditional hypothesis: where parties are materially interdependent, at least one will not yet settle ultimate territorial status, and a minimal guarantor capacity exists, legally protected functional institutions can improve service continuity without agreement on status. It introduces the Universal Framework for Divided Sovereignty (UFDS), which unbundles sovereignty into five functional pillars (identity charters, property and infrastructure boards, municipal security units, algorithmic fiscal clearing, and shared-site administration) and entrenches them under a status non-prejudice clause. The claimed contribution is integration, not invention. Each component has precedent; UFDS combines them around a distinct sequencing principle, function before status, with an explicit legal architecture, adversarial failure protocols, and falsifiable hypotheses. The paper compares UFDS with federal, confederal, consociational, autonomy, and joint-management arrangements and identifies the narrow problem for which each is insufficient. It specifies the legal instruments and the constitutional questions they raise, models six forms of strategic abuse and the framework's behaviour when safeguards fail, and proposes indicators, comparators, and simulation designs, while stating that simulation cannot establish how real actors will behave. Applications to Kashmir and Israel-Palestine, Lebanon, and Nigeria show where the proposition is most and least plausible.

detail.abstract: Metal-phenolic networks (MPNs) provide modular, coordination-driven coatings, but they rely on metal centers and are usually amorphous organic-metal hybrids. Silicate-phenolic networks (SPNs) extend this concept by using silicate as an inorganic node that is linked through dynamic covalent coordination to phenolic ligands such as tannic acid, gallic acid, and pyrogallol. Recent work shows that such coatings can encapsulate small molecules, including urea, and that their surface hydrophobicity and metal-ion content can be tuned to control release. This review synthesizes the literature on MPN chemistry, silicate solution chemistry, and encapsulation and release from coated particles, and examines how these strands combine in hybrid silicate-metal-phenolic systems. We distinguish reported findings, such as pH-and hydrophobicity-dependent urea release from SPN coatings and post-assembly loading with Fe, Cu, and Zn, from hypotheses about assembly mechanism and structure. Gaps are identified in molecular-level structural characterization, in the role of ionic strength and solution speciation, and in kinetic modeling and field validation. We propose a four-parameter conceptual framework relating ligand, silicate and metal composition, surface functionalization, and environment to surface properties and encapsulation performance, expressed as testable hypotheses rather than results. We conclude with priorities for mechanistic study, independent replication, and sustainability assessment, and we state explicitly which claims rest on published evidence and which on interpretation.

detail.abstract: Plants release polyphenols into the soil, where they meet minerals, metal ions, and microbial communities. Soil science has long recognized that organic ligands can bind mineral surfaces, promote dissolution, and influence the persistence of organic matter, but the role of phenolic ligands in controlling the crystallinity of minerals has received far less attention. Recent work reports that tannic acid, a catechol-rich polyphenol, can mobilize metals and phosphorus from soil minerals, be incorporated into newly formed hybrid minerals, and lower the crystallinity of calcium phosphate and struvite, with downstream effects on nutrient release and crop growth. Parallel work on engineered phenolic coordination assemblies shows that related chemistry can be used to build pHresponsive coatings that release nutrients in soil. This review synthesizes the literature on phenolic coordination chemistry, ligand-mineral interactions, crystallization pathways, rhizosphere processes, and phosphate and metal cycling. We separate reported findings from interpretation, identify gaps in mechanism, scale, and field validation, and propose a four-process conceptual framework linking complexation, dissolution, reprecipitation, and biological response, expressed as testable hypotheses rather than results. We conclude with research priorities for independent replication, realistic dosing, persistence studies, and environmental assessment, including the risk of mobilizing unwanted metals. Throughout, reported findings are kept distinct from interpretation.

detail.abstract: Based on a comprehensive visual deception score constructed from China's mandatorily disclosed IPO roadshow videos using computer vision and machine learning, we find that visual cues embedded in these videos predict IPO financial fraud. The predictive power is incremental to financial, textual, and audio indicators. Further analyses show that these cues are well grounded in psychology research and focusing on the psychology-based deception-cue-area features improves fraud predicting performance. Furthermore, decomposing each video into five topics, we find that only the deception score of the topic on financial performance is positively associated with financial fraud. We further show that insiders of firms with higher visual deception scores are more likely to sell shares shortly after lock-up periods expire, and these firms experience significantly lower subsequent stock returns. Our study demonstrates the feasibility and potential value of using video information for fraud detection in accounting and finance.

detail.abstract: Performance management has become an essential organizational practice for improving employee productivity, institutional accountability, and organizational effectiveness. In Bangladesh, however, the implementation of effective performance management systems faces multiple structural, cultural, administrative, and organizational challenges. This paper explores the major challenges of performance management practices in Bangladesh across both public and private sector organizations. The study discusses key issues related to goal setting, performance indicators, employee feedback, organizational culture, leadership practices, resource limitations, and institutional barriers. Particular attention is given to the influence of cultural values, bureaucratic structures, political interference, and resistance to organizational change on performance management effectiveness. The paper further examines the challenges of employee development, performance evaluation, and accountability mechanisms within the Bangladeshi context. In addition, the study highlights possible strategic responses and policy recommendations for improving performance management systems through institutional reforms, capacity building, technological modernization, training, and performance-based organizational culture. The findings suggest that although performance management practices in Bangladesh are evolving gradually, substantial improvements are needed to establish transparent, fair, and development-oriented systems capable of enhancing organizational performance and employee effectiveness.

detail.abstract: Since 2021 Pakistan has built its retail payments policy around Raast, an instant payment system owned and operated by the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP). Through regulatory circulars the SBP has required banks, microfinance banks and electronic money institutions to connect to Raast, to read a single QR standard, to support person-to-merchant payments and, from 2025, to deploy a digital acceptance solution for every business customer. This article asks under what conditions such mandatory interoperability improves competition and consumer welfare, and what regulatory costs and risks it creates. It develops a four-layer framework that separates the shared rail from the account, customer-facing and merchantacquiring layers in which rivalry actually occurs, and from the economics of network effects, two-sided markets, switching costs and regulatory design it derives five conditions under which interoperability can be expected to translate into effective competition: neutral access, sustainable pricing, a contestable customer-facing layer, aligned liability for fraud and security, and separated governance supported by evidence. The framework is applied to Pakistan's statutory and regulatory instruments and to published SBP statistics, and is set against the European Union's Instant Payments Regulation and its treatment of mobile-wallet access, India's Unified Payments Interface and the controversy over its market-share cap, Brazil's Pix, and the evidence on mobile-money interoperability in Africa. The analysis finds that interoperability has clearly expanded reach and volume, especially for person-to-person transfers, but that the public record does not yet permit any conclusion about competition: merchant-side use remains small, provider-level data are unpublished, and the SBP's combined roles as owner, operator and regulator of the rail raise governance questions. The article proposes a staged, evidence-driven agenda for the SBP and the Competition Commission of Pakistan.

title: Trust Across Scale: Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) as Renormalisation

detail.title: Trust Across Scale: Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) as Renormalisation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: Trust appears to involve an assent that institutions cannot command. Yet institutions organise relationships in which participation, obligation and dependence frequently precede assent. This tension between the apparent volition of trust and the compulsion of institutions supplies the foundation for an enquiry into public-private partnership (PPP) across scales. The ultraviolet (UV) identifies local interactions through which participants disclose information, exercise judgement and entrust consequential interests to others. The infrared (IR) identifies extensive arrangements of law, procurement and public authority. Wilsonian effective actions, coarse-graining maps and scale-flow equations frame the effective structure of interaction as resolution changes. Projected dynamics identify the memory that a reduced account must preserve. Sociology reveals why that structure cannot be reduced to voluntary exchange, contractual enforcement or a uniform quantity of trust. Drawing on Durkheim, Bourdieu, Baier, Luhmann, Giddens and Möllering, the paper develops the proposition that institutions organise vulnerability while trust concerns how participants inhabit relationships of vulnerability. The British movement from early Private Finance Initiative arrangements towards the partnering agenda advanced under New Labour provides a historical investigation of policy acting upon local relationships. Improved construction performance supports the possibility of consequential IR-to-UV intervention, without establishing universal cultural transformation or attributing the achievement to one government alone. PPP emerges as an adaptive institutional operator whose public value depends on the organisation of knowledge, discretion and accountability across scales.

title: Institutional Execution Infrastructure: Bridging the Gap between Intelligence and Institutional Execution

detail.title: Institutional Execution Infrastructure: Bridging the Gap between Intelligence and Institutional Execution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, commercial, or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could be perceived to have inappropriately influenced or biased the research, conceptual frameworks, or findings presented in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is purely conceptual, architectural, and theoretical in nature, and did not involve human participants, clinical trials, or animal subjects.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is significantly reducing the cost of generating hypotheses, analyses, predictions, recommendations, and candidate actions. Yet across complex, highly regulated environments, the ability to generate machine intelligence does not automatically translate into the ability to execute it. Organizational throughput remains fundamentally constrained by authorization structures, procedural dependencies, institutional friction, verification requirements, governance capacity, and the systemic difficulty of preserving expert knowledge across changing personnel, software applications, and technology platforms. As machine learning systems expand beyond purely digital interfaces into physical, financial, and operational systems that perceive and act upon the real world, the distinction between intelligence generation and reliable execution becomes increasingly consequential. This paper proposes that these operational constraints constitute a distinct institutional execution infrastructure problem.

To address this challenge, the paper synthesizes and extends three related lines of foundational work. First, the Legal Friction Index™ (LFI™) provides a diagnostic perspective for identifying, measuring, and analyzing legal, administrative, and institutional friction. Second, Role-Based Legal Cognition Modeling™ (RLCM™), together with Institutional Cognitive Compression™ (ICC™), addresses how recurring institutional reasoning and procedural logic can be formally represented through roles, explicit authority, constraints, procedures, exception pathways, and escalation mechanisms. Third, Structural Capital Intelligence™ (SCI™) examines the economic significance of structural control, execution rights, technological dependency, and the durability of value. The present paper brings these theoretical and practical perspectives together into a comprehensive framework: Institutional Execution Infrastructure™ (IEI™).

IEI is proposed as an institutional and technical architecture for governing the transition from machine-generated possibilities to fully authorized, constrained, executed, and verifiable outcomes. A central thesis of the framework is that the intelligence generation layer—encompassing language models, neural networks, or hybrid systems—must be decoupled from the infrastructure governing consequential action. The framework does not require probabilistic models to achieve internal determinism. Instead, it demonstrates how permissions, prerequisites, state transitions, and verification requirements can be enforced through separately governed, deterministic mechanisms.

The framework distinguishes five explicit execution states: generated, accepted, authorized, executed, and verified, establishing that raw intelligence output is not valid execution evidence. It introduces the Evergreen Institutional Expertise Asset™ (EIEA™) as a proposed representation of validated institutional knowledge that is persistent, versioned, governed, portable, composable, auditable, and capable of controlled evolution. It defines the Execution Infrastructure Gap™ (EIG™) as the variance between required and actually demonstrated execution outcomes, positioning LFI as a diagnostic instrument for isolating friction contributing to that gap. Furthermore, it details a closed-loop architecture linking capital assessment, friction measurement, expertise representation, governed execution, real-time verification, system telemetry, and controlled iterative improvement.

Although engineered from institutional, legal, and administrative applications, IEI extends directly to adjacent domains requiring pre-execution controls, including physical AI (robotics) and financial technology (payment processing). The paper concludes with formal propositions, evaluation methods, and explicit limitations intended to open the framework to rigorous empirical testing.

detail.abstract: The US-China trade war of 2018-2019 was expected to benefit third countries that could replace Chinese goods in the US market. This paper asks which Indian manufacturing workers the tariffs reached, and whether employment or its terms changed where they landed. I link product-level tariff changes to six rounds of India's labour force surveys, estimating four tariff sets jointly: the US tariffs on China, China's retaliation, China's tariff cuts for other partners and the US tariffs on India. Exposure to the US tariffs on China predicts export growth to the United States but not detectably to the rest of the world, although the estimate is precise only when weighted by export value. The tariffs reached industries that employ few women: the most exposed industries are less than half as female as the rest under every cutoff examined (6% against 36% at the quartile), a gap present in 2011-12. Caste composition does not vary with exposure. Exposure shows no detectable association with industry employment shares, regular wages or four measures of formal employment terms, for any caste group. Estimating fewer tariff sets produces significant caste-specific associations that pass their own pre-period test but lose significance once all four sets enter.

title: The Ghost of Philip Waki: Has Kenya Outgrown, or Merely Institutionalized, State-Sponsored Goonism?

detail.title: The Ghost of Philip Waki: Has Kenya Outgrown, or Merely Institutionalized, State-Sponsored Goonism?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NONE

detail.abstract: On 15 October 2008, Justice Philip Waki delivered to President Mwai Kibaki and the Panel of Eminent African Personalities a 529-page indictment of Kenya's political culture: the Report of the Commission of Inquiry into Post-Election Violence (CIPEV), which determined that the deaths of at least 1,133 Kenyans following the 2007 election were attributable not to spontaneous ethnic conflict but to organised, financed and politically orchestrated violence, executed substantially by gangs recruited and remunerated by political and commercial elites. Seventeen years later, on 12 July 2026, armed men uniformly characterised in police statements and press reportage as "goons" assailed a church service and a political rally in Kisumu and Nyahururu respectively, days ahead of a parliamentary by-election in Ol Kalou, while the state security apparatus constitutionally obliged to safeguard both assemblies either failed to discharge that duty or, on credible allegation, acquiesced in its breach. This article interrogates the question its title poses directly: has Kenya outgrown the mechanism Waki diagnosed, or has it merely institutionalised it? Testing that question against the successive collapse of the domestic Special Tribunal and the International Criminal Court process, the documented recurrence of hired political violence across three subsequent electoral cycles, Kenya's constitutional guarantees under Articles 21, 37 and 244, and the 84.1 per cent probability of electoral violence a 2026 statistical index now assigns to 2027, the article concludes that Kenya has not outgrown its ghost. It has, rather, furnished the ghost a permanent address, and continues to service the tenancy.

detail.abstract: Organisations seldom fail through a single visible defect. In mature organisations, deterioration can accumulate through administrative burden, friction in decision-making, weakened execution, financial dysfunction, strategic rigidity and defensive behaviour. This paper sets out the foundation of a diagnostic programme that examines such conditions through separate, transparent heuristic indices, and defines the vocabulary on which the later papers of the series rely. It defines what 'organisational failure' and 'fragility' mean in this programme, and proposes three constructs: the Compliance Density Index (CDI), which relates compliance and documentation effort to execution effort; the Committee Inflation Index (CII), which relates the person-time consumed by committee processes to decision output against a stated reference; and the Composite Organisational Fragility Index (COFI), a four-dimension composite whose dimensions are defined, normalised and fed by indicators proposed in Papers II to V. The paper revises the earlier edition by removing underived alert levels for CDI and CII, rebuilding CII on person-hours per decision, giving COFI computable components and a non-compensatory companion reading, and adding literature positioning, synthetic worked examples and a validation programme. The constructs are screening lenses. They indicate where investigation might begin; they do not establish failure, misconduct or causation. No empirical results are reported.

detail.abstract: Agricultural chemicals, including fertilizers and pesticides, are applied in large quantities, and much of what is applied is lost before it reaches its target. Coating or encapsulating the active ingredient can slow its release, but many coatings are made from synthetic polymers that persist in soil and raise concern about microplastic accumulation. Metal-phenolic networks (MPNs), formed by coordination between plant polyphenols and metal ions, are a bio-derived coating chemistry with tunable properties. Recent work has adapted MPN chemistry to urea, through nonaqueous assembly, solvent-free mechanochemistry, and silicate-phenolic networks, and has reported pH-and hydrophobicity-dependent release in soil. A related study reports that polyphenol-mineral hybrids can increase nutrient release and crop growth. This review synthesizes the literature on MPN coatings, the degradation of tannins and polymer coatings in soil, and controlled release of agrochemicals, and asks what is established about biodegradability. We find that release has been demonstrated while biodegradation has been addressed only indirectly, and that applications beyond fertilizers remain largely unexplored. We propose a design framework linking coating composition, release, degradation, and environmental assessment, expressed as testable hypotheses rather than results. We conclude with priorities for standardized degradation testing, extension to pesticides, metal-safety assessment, and independent replication across laboratories and soils.

title: Business Planning in The New Economy of Uzbekistan: Institutional Shifts, Macroeconomic Constraints and an Adaptive Planning Framework

detail.title: Business Planning in The New Economy of Uzbekistan: Institutional Shifts, Macroeconomic Constraints and an Adaptive Planning Framework

detail.abstract: Since 2017 Uzbekistan has moved from a state-directed model towards a market-oriented economy, and the conditions under which firms plan, finance and scale their operations have changed accordingly. This article examines how business planning should be adapted to the “new economy” of Uzbekistan, understood as an environment of rapid growth, tight monetary policy, liberalised foreign trade and frequent regulatory change. Using desk research and triangulation of official statistics (National Statistics Committee, Central Bank, Ministry of Investments, Industry and Trade) with assessments of the World Bank Group, the Asian Development Bank and the WTO accession process, the study documents five stylised facts: (i) real GDP growth of 7.7% in 2025 accompanied by an implied nominal GDP deflator of about 11.9%; (ii) a decline in the official share of small business and private entrepreneurship in GDP from 67.4% in 2017 to 52.2% in 2025, below the 55% policy target; (iii) persistently tight monetary conditions, with a 14% policy rate and 6.2% annual inflation in August 2026; (iv) record foreign investment and loans of USD 43.1 billion in 2025 coexisting with a state-owned enterprise footprint above 30% of GDP; and (v) a dense 2025–2026 reform calendar, including a new small-business tax package and advanced WTO accession talks. On this basis the article proposes an Adaptive Business Planning Framework (ABPF) consisting of five modules – policy-calendar scan, sector–region segmentation, scenario-based financial planning, compliance-and-digital layer, and scale-up pathway – and formulates four testable propositions. The framework is intended for entrepreneurs, SME advisers and regional policymakers.

detail.abstract: We examine whether temporarily assigning employees to high-opportunity contexts can improve their productivity after returning to lower-opportunity settings. Using transaction data from a multi-store restaurant chain, we compare the productivity of servers in the general dining area (a context with limited opportunity for sales and tips) before and after a temporary assignment to the lounge section (a highopportunity context). We find that the temporary reassignment increased treated servers' hourly sales in subsequent periods, and the treatment effects could be attributed to skill improvement and motivation enhancement. However, the treatment effects were heterogeneous among servers: Only about half of the treated servers increased their productivity both during and after the treatment, whereas the other half experienced reduced productivity during the treatment and merely recovered their pre-treatment productivity after the treatment. Finally, despite the heterogeneous treatment effects on productivity, all treated servers experienced lower exit rates than those in the control group. These findings suggest that temporary opportunity assignments can potentially develop employee skills and enhance employee motivation, thereby improving employee productivity. The treatment also improves employee retention regardless of treatment outcomes. Our findings speak to the literature on how organization design affects employee productivity.

detail.abstract: We investigate a newsvendor problem where a decision-maker observes a z-dimensional vector of covariates, and wants to learn how much stock to order given a sample of size n of censored demand data to minimize costs. Demand is censored when insufficient stock is available to meet it, and past stocking quantities are known. We propose a new model-agnostic loss function approach to estimate optimal order quantities using observational data, and characterize the optimal newsvendor policy as the policy that minimizes our proposed loss function. Our method requires only a single estimation step, can be scaled to datasets with hundreds of thousands of data points, and does not suffer from the same instabilities as inverse censoring probability weighting methods. We describe how this loss function can be implemented in linear empirical risk minimization, kernel weights optimization and deep neural network algorithms, and provide excess risk generalization bounds for their out-of-sample performance. Moreover, we show through numerical experiments that our method quickly converges to the optimal policy on synthetic data, and leads to improved performance on real world retail data.

title: Absorptive Capacity, AI-Based Decision Support, and Administrative Decision-Making Effectiveness in Public Sector Organizations: A Systematic Review and Integrative Framework for the Saudi Context

detail.title: Absorptive Capacity, AI-Based Decision Support, and Administrative Decision-Making Effectiveness in Public Sector Organizations: A Systematic Review and Integrative Framework for the Saudi Context

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a systematic review of published literature and did not involve human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Purpose. Public organizations are adopting AI-based decision support systems (AI-DSS) on the assumption that they will improve administrative decisions, yet the organizational capability needed to absorb external knowledge and turn it into better decisions is rarely examined. This review asks whether absorptive capacity (ACAP) is associated with AI-DSS adoption and with administrative decision-making effectiveness (ADME), whether AI-DSS carries an effect of ACAP on ADME, and what the evidence implies for Saudi public administration. Design/methodology/approach. A systematic literature review following SPAR-4-SLR, PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S, with synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM). An open multidisciplinary scholarly database (OpenAlex) was searched on 28 September 2026 with 12 query families, supplemented by a candidate list and a pilot search. Explicit construct-equivalence rules separated direct from adjacent evidence. Quality was appraised with the MMAT, and certainty with GRADE and GRADE-CERQual criteria. Screening and extraction were carried out by one reviewer supported by a large language model under written decision rules. Findings. Of 8,260 records (6,480 after deduplication), 525 reports were sought, 199 were assessed in full and 61 studies were included. No study tested the full ACAP → AI-DSS → ADME chain. Only five studies measured ACAP directly, and the three statistical tests of ACAP on technology adoption found small or marginal associations. Of 12 inferential studies linking AI or analytics use to a direct decision outcome, eight reported positive, two null, one mixed and one conditional associations; all positive findings rested on cross-sectional self-reports, and the three studies that observed decisions directly were less favourable. The strongest evidence (23 studies, moderate certainty) concerned the conditions of AI-supported decisions: discretion, accountability, trust, data quality, power and leadership attention. Only three included studies were Saudi. Research limitations/implications. One database was searched, 326 of 525 reports could not be read in full and no second reviewer took part. Future research should validate public-sector ACAP measures, observe decision outcomes directly and test the mediation chain longitudinally. Practical implications. AI procurement alone is unlikely to improve administrative decisions. Saudi agencies should build knowledge-absorbing routines, design accountable discretion and measure decision outcomes. Originality/value. This is the first review to integrate organizational absorptive capacity, AI-based decision support and decision effectiveness in one public-sector evidence base. It shows that the proposed mediation model is untested and offers a conditional framework with testable propositions for the Saudi context.

detail.abstract: Metal-phenolic networks (MPNs) are coordination-driven materials that assemble from phenolic ligands and metal ions into films, capsules, particles, and coatings. Their appeal lies in modularity, since the metal, the ligand, and the assembly conditions can all be varied. Yet the relationships connecting these design variables to network structure, and network structure to properties such as stability, mechanical behavior, wettability, charge, and release, are scattered across studies that differ in substrate, solvent, and measurement. This review synthesizes the literature on MPN assembly, coordination chemistry principles relevant to metal and ligand selection, and recent work extending MPNs to nonaqueous, solvent-free, silicate-containing, and mineral-hybrid systems. We distinguish reported findings, such as pH-responsive disassembly and tunable mechanical properties, from inferences drawn from general coordination chemistry. Gaps are identified in quantitative descriptors of network structure, in controlled comparison across variables, and in standardized reporting. We propose a three-axis conceptual framework mapping metal, ligand, and assembly conditions onto structural descriptors and properties, expressed as testable hypotheses rather than results. We conclude with priorities for systematic variation, improved characterization, and independent replication, so that MPN design can move from empirical exploration toward prediction. Throughout, reported findings are kept separate from interpretation and from proposed future work.

title: Who Decides When the Machine Thinks? Full Human Control Over High-Impact Corporate Decisions and Corporate Responsibility Under Kuwaiti and Comparative Law

detail.title: Who Decides When the Machine Thinks? Full Human Control Over High-Impact Corporate Decisions and Corporate Responsibility Under Kuwaiti and Comparative Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no one

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming integral to corporate decision-making. The legal difficulty is no longer limited to whether automated acts can be attributed to an enterprise; it also concerns the boundary between automated assistance and human decisional authority. This Article advances a proposition more demanding than the familiar requirement to keep a human "in the loop": where a high-impact corporate decision is designated for human judgment, an authorized natural person must retain the whole of the final decisionmaking authority. That person must personally assess the material evidence, consider the available alternatives and their consequences, and expressly select the course of action before execution. AI may research, analyze, compare options, and formulate recommendations, but it must not displace the human's final evaluative judgment. The question is especially important under Kuwaiti law. Law No. 20 of 2014 Concerning Electronic Transactions expressly recognizes automated electronic systems. Article 8 permits legally effective contracts to be concluded through such systems without the direct or personal intervention of a natural person in the formation process, subject to the statutory conditions. Article 11 provides for the attribution of electronic documents and records generated by systems configured to operate automatically. This Article therefore does not contend that full human intervention is already a general condition of contractual validity in Kuwait. Instead, it proposes a targeted corporate-governance requirement governing how enterprises authorize highimpact decisions without disturbing the rights of third parties under otherwise valid automated transactions. The analysis situates that proposal alongside Kuwait's Civil Code rules on liability for wrongful acts, Law No. 1 of 2016 on Companies, and the corporate-governance framework administered by the Capital Markets Authority. Comparative reference is made to the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and the UNCITRAL Model Law on Automated Contracting, without asserting that either already imposes full human decision-making in every case. The Article introduces the Full Human Decision Rule (FHDR) as a proposed standard for defined categories of high-impact corporate decisions. Under the FHDR, a decision is not fully human merely because an employee clicks "approve." The enterprise must identify the human decision-maker, give that person direct access to material facts rather than only an AI-generated summary, afford adequate time and competence for an independent assessment of alternatives, preserve actual authority to reject, amend, defer, or escalate the recommendation, and require an affirmative, proportionately reasoned, auditable human decision before execution. "Full" describes the allocation of final decisional authority; it does not prohibit AI-assisted preparation or the automated execution of an independently approved decision.

detail.abstract: Thin coatings that combine polyphenols with silicate chemistry have been reported as a means of encapsulating small molecules and releasing them in a controlled manner (Mazaheri et al., 2024). The performance of such coatings is determined not only by bulk composition but also by the interfaces they contain: between payload and coating, between the phenolic and silicate components within the coating, and between the coating and its surrounding medium. Despite their importance, these interfaces have rarely been treated as design targets. This review draws on the literature on polyphenol and metal-phenolic assembly, silica surface chemistry, layer-by-layer film engineering, and diffusioncontrolled release to construct an interface-centred account of silicate-phenolic coatings. It distinguishes principles established in adjacent fields from hypotheses specific to silicate-phenolic hybrids, for which direct evidence is limited. Key gaps are identified, including the absence of agreed interfacial descriptors, limited understanding of how phenolic and silicate phases interact, and a lack of release studies in realistic media. A conceptual framework is proposed that treats the three interfaces as engineering levers and links them to measurable descriptors and to five testable hypotheses. The review argues that deliberate interfacial design, supported by shared characterisation standards, is a more efficient route to dependable encapsulation performance than formulation-by-trial, and it outlines priorities for experimental work.

detail.abstract: Asylum coordination in South America has remained largely distinct from models promoted elsewhere in the world, with transfer-based schemes emerging only in recent years. This study traces the evolution of the region's solidarity-based regime of refugee protection, rooted in the 1984 Cartagena Declaration and intra-regional free movement frameworks, toward a hemispheric, deterrence-oriented model championed by North American states under the 2022 Los Angeles Declaration. It focuses on the U.S.-Paraguay transfer agreement signed in August 2025, one of the first such agreements in the region. Drawing on official documents and public statements, the study combines migration diplomacy with a neo-institutional approach to argue that the emergence of transfer-based asylum coordination cannot be explained solely by hemispheric power asymmetries or foreign policy interests. The Paraguayan case shows how this shift is also shaped by domestic institutional trajectories, including organizational preferences and capacities, as well as the uneven historical influence of international organizations, particularly the International Organization for Migration (IOM), and non-governmental actors. More broadly, the study highlights the importance of institutions and historical legacies for understanding how asymmetric interstate relations and a shifting regional political context are reshaping refugee protection in South America.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence gives Africa an unusual development opportunity. Airports, highways, railways, and hospitals are bound by geography and national borders. AI capability is different. It can be designed from the start to work across institutions and countries. Yet Africa risks repeating, in its new AI ecosystem, the same fragmentation that has long held back its physical infrastructure. Countries may build national AI strategies, data centers, innovation hubs, and training programs that have no real way to share capability across borders. This Viewpoint argues that Africa should not build fifty-four isolated AI ecosystems and try to bridge them later. The bridges belong in the architecture from the start. Building on the African Union's Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy and its Digital Transformation Strategy for Africa (African Union, 2020, 2024), the author proposes the Shared African AI Ecosystem Framework (SAAIEF). In this framework, compute, data governance, talent, knowledge, cybersecurity, and economic opportunity work as connected regional capabilities rather than purely national assets. The framework treats servant leadership as AI infrastructure. Leaders and institutions must be willing to invest in capability whose benefits reach beyond their own organizations and borders. The central claim is simple. AI adoption is not Africa's development outcome. Productive capacity, better public services, African innovation, jobs, knowledge creation, and shared prosperity are the outcomes that matter. The coordination gap is documented, not speculative. As of July 2025, only 16 of Africa's 54 countries had published a national AI strategy (Intelpoint, 2025). The continent holds less than 1% of global data-center capacity for 1.4 billion people (Adepetun, 2026). An estimated 38% of African developers work for at least one foreign company (Lemma, 2025). Yet the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), which now links more than 30 African countries, shows that shared continental digital infrastructure already works (Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, 2026). African AI infrastructure should be built the same way.

detail.abstract: In commodity futures markets, basis and basis momentum capture carry but compress the term structure into scalar projections, obscuring where front-end distortions occur across maturities and how they evolve over time. We address this measurement problem by encoding each commodity's recent futures curve as an ordered time-maturity surface and using a convolutional neural network to estimate two surface-filtered carry predictors, bs_DV and bm_DV, supervised on future carry measures rather than returns. The predictors contain incremental carry information and significantly predict returns beyond standard controls. Factors constructed from the predictors improve the mean-variance frontier, earn positive risk premia, and reduce pricing errors beyond standard commodity factors. To interpret the economic intuition of bs_DV and bm_DV , we develop a storage-based model in which inventory scarcity generates local front-end distortions that propagate across adjacent maturities, linking the patterns extracted by convolution to expected carry dynamics.

detail.abstract: Online social networks have become important platforms for communication, information exchange, business promotion, and public engagement. However, their growing popularity has also created opportunities for spam accounts, automated bots, fraudulent profiles, and coordinated malicious communities to operate at scale. These accounts frequently exploit the relationships between legitimate users to distribute misleading information, promote suspicious websites, manipulate engagement statistics, and conduct phishing attacks. Conventional detection techniques that examine individual messages or account characteristics may fail to recognize coordinated activities involving multiple profiles. Graph-based data mining offers an alternative approach by representing users as nodes and their relationships as edges, making it possible to investigate suspicious patterns across the wider network. This article proposes a graph-based framework for identifying spam accounts and suspicious communities through network construction, structural feature extraction, community detection, and machine learning classification. The framework combines measures such as degree centrality, clustering coefficient, interaction frequency, community density, and behavioral similarity to identify accounts that may be participating in coordinated abuse. It also incorporates temporal analysis to examine how suspicious relationships and activities develop over time. The proposed approach is discussed in relation to detection accuracy, scalability, interpretability, privacy, and the challenges associated with evolving spam strategies. The framework provides a foundation for developing more reliable social network security systems that can investigate both individual accounts and organized groups without treating unusual network behavior as conclusive evidence of malicious activity.

detail.abstract: Drawing on interviews with Nuon Chea (1926-2019) and former members of the Communist Party of Thailand (CPT), together with contemporary publications and surviving educational and administrative records, this study reconstructs Nuon Chea's life and political activities in Bangkok between 1942 and 1950. It also examines a significant transformation in the social composition of Thailand's communist movement in the late 1940s: the broadening of its base from an established leadership composed largely of Thailand-born activists of Chinese ancestry to include a somewhat younger generation of Thai intellectuals educated within the Thai school system. By identifying Nuon Chea's Thai name, Runglert Laodi, and tracing his education at Wat Benjamabopit School and Thammasat University, his employment in the Thai civil service, and his involvement in the Thai Youth Organization, the study corrects substantial inaccuracies in earlier accounts of his political development. It establishes that he became involved in the Thai Youth Organization in 1947, not 1944, and that he did not formally join the CPT until 1950, shortly before leaving Thailand to take part in the anti-colonial struggle in Cambodia. Beyond reconstructing Nuon Chea's early political career, the study investigates the activities and personal networks of Thai intellectuals associated with the CPT, including Ruam Wongphan, Prasoet Sapsunthon, Sanoh Phanitcharoen, Somkhwan Phichaikul, and Udom Charoenrat. Their educational backgrounds, political experiences, and ties to established communist activists show how the party and its affiliated organizations drew in a new generation of Thai intellectuals in the early postwar years. The study pays particular attention to the roles of student organizations, political publications, personal contacts, and recruitment networks in facilitating this broadening. By examining Nuon Chea's political development alongside that of his Thai contemporaries, the study elucidates in concrete terms the process by which Thai intellectuals entered and became active in Thailand's communist movement in the late 1940s. It thereby contributes not only to a more accurate understanding of Nuon Chea's formative years but also to the social and organizational history of the CPT during a period of marked generational change.

detail.abstract: Food supply networks consist of complex, intertwined relationships among firms that depend on each other for flows of goods and services. Even in "commodity" markets, transactions between firms involve contracts and long-term relationships in which prices and other terms are set through a negotiation process, so bargaining power is key. Importantly, the stability of these relationships determines the resilience of the entire network through disruptions that may interrupt the normal flow of goods and services. We estimate the importance of bargaining power and network relationships for the resilience of an important food supply chain-bananas. We find that bargaining power is critically important in determining the length of supply relationships, particularly in interaction with the network location of the buyer, seller, or the dyad itself. We find that network ties are not nearly as fragile as models of supply chain resilience in the macroeconomics and supply chain management literatures suggest. More importantly, we find that greater bargaining power and more central or proximate locations in the network interact to produce greater supply stability than would otherwise be the case. Contrary to policies designed to address supply chain resilience, large, important firms with bargaining power may promote supply chain resilience, rather than detract from it as commonly assumed.

detail.abstract: Unplanned absenteeism disrupts production planning in labor-intensive garment factories, yet few studies examine whether the physical work environment shapes it. This study tests whether access to natural daylight relates to unplanned absenteeism among industrial workers. I analyzed six months of biometric attendance data (April to September 2026) from Agami Apparels Ltd., a high-headcount manufacturing facility in Savar, Dhaka, Bangladesh. I extracted records from ZKBio Time hardware using T-SQL, restricted the sample to active employees, and compared monthly unplanned absenteeism between two shift groups: the General Shift, which works under daylight, and the Day Night Shift, which relies entirely on artificial light. The General Shift recorded lower absenteeism in every month of the study period. In July 2026, the peak monsoon month, the Day Night Shift reached 2.09% absenteeism against 1.25% for the General Shift. The gap peaked in September 2026, when the Day Night Shift recorded 2.77% and the General Shift 1.50%. These patterns align with the circadian and immune-health literature, which links daylight exposure to sleep regulation and physiological resilience. The observational design cannot establish causation, and unmeasured differences between the shifts may contribute to the gap. Even so, the consistency of the difference across six months gives factory managers a practical signal. I recommend that HR teams review shift rotation rules, that facility planners evaluate daylight access in production areas, and that future studies add individual-level health and sleep measures.
