detail.abstract: With electricity storage assets becoming an essential complement to the growth of intermittent renewable generation, there is increasing policy interest in providing market arrangements to de-risk their operations. We design a competitive spread-limit product that lowers the operational risk for electricity storage operators competing in the day ahead auctions. Storage participation in the auctions are thereby facilitated without having to incur the forecasting risk of pre-specifying charging and discharging hours, or asset-specific parameters. A bidder submits a capacity and a minimum acceptable daily spread; the exchange accepts capacity in merit order, constructs one or more optimal intertemporal profiles and allocates pro rata across accepted units. Settlement ensures that every accepted order recovers its submitted spread limit. We further show that the aggregate consumer-plus-producer surplus of the non-storage participants is weakly higher than in the no-storage benchmark, The welfare of a stepwise order book admits an exact linear representation, which yields an LP-first clearing formulation. Using 2020-2024 order-book data from seven European markets, we find that multi-cycle flexibility raises the welfare gain from storage relative to a one-cycle benchmark and raises the non-storage surplus gain in every market-month. The design offers a standardized and transparent way to integrate storage flexibility.

detail.abstract: Fraud detection in enterprise resource planning (ERP) environments is increasingly constrained by transaction volume, event velocity, heterogeneous business processes, and the adaptive behavior of fraud actors. SAP S/4HANA integrates financial, procurement, sales, supply-chain, asset, and master-data processes, creating an environment in which a suspicious event may only become meaningful when it is interpreted in relation to preceding transactions, entity history, user behavior, and business context. This study develops a benchmark-driven and architecture-oriented framework for artificial-intelligence (AI) fraud detection in SAP S/4HANA, combining supervised transaction classification, anomaly detection, rule evidence, real-time event processing, composite risk scoring, explainability, and human investigation. Because confidential SAP production transactions were not available, the empirical component uses the publicly documented PaySim synthetic financial-transaction benchmark as secondary data. PaySim contains 6,362,620 transactions, including 8,213 fraudulent transactions, yielding a fraud prevalence of approximately 0.1291%. Published benchmark evidence is analyzed rather than represented as a newly generated SAP experiment. In the benchmark, standard XGBoost reported ROC-AUC of 0.9350 and F1 of 0.8410, whereas random-under-sampling combined with XGBoost reported ROC-AUC of 0.9955 and recall of 0.9976 but precision of 0.1637. These differences demonstrate that model selection cannot be reduced to a single performance metric in a highly imbalanced operational environment. Building on the evidence, the paper proposes an SAP S/4HANA architecture in which business events are enriched with behavioral features, scored by supervised and anomaly models, combined with deterministic detection evidence, and converted into a 0-100 risk score that supports configurable decision thresholds. The framework further incorporates probability calibration, concept-drift monitoring, model versioning, SHAP-oriented explanations, investigation feedback, and audit logging. The study contributes a practical bridge between fraud-detection research and enterprise ERP implementation by showing how public benchmark evidence can inform a governed real-time monitoring architecture without claiming access to proprietary SAP transaction data.

detail.abstract: Agentic processes increasingly combine AI agents, tools, persistent state, delegated authority, external systems, and human oversight. Their operation can generate large volumes of heterogeneous telemetry, security findings, audit records, testing results, and incident evidence, but neither volume nor technical success alone establishes compliance beyond the specific policy, control, and assessment scope actually evaluated. This paper develops and specifies an evidence-governed assessment model for agentic processes. It addresses three research questions concerning claim-preserving control mapping, bounded compliance assessment, and selective promotion of high-volume observations into active governance workflows. First, the model defines a claim-preserving specialization of established evidence-to-assessment practice for heterogeneous agentic evidence. Second, it defines an evidence-governed promotion chain that separates evidence preservation from workflow activation so that retained telemetry does not automatically become an active GRC object. Third, it places these semantics in an interoperable plan-do-check-act lifecycle that connects controlled testing, runtime monitoring, intrusion response, investigation-derived evidence, remediation, retesting, reassessment, and existing enterprise GRC platforms through a platform-neutral semantic interface. The model uses five typed control-assessment states: Supported, Contradicted, Insufficient evidence, Unresolved, and Not applicable. It also specifies bounded exchange records and a worked approvalbefore-payment example. The central claim boundary is that security and assurance evidence may support and, where an authorized assessment method defines a closed technical control objective and the required observation conditions are satisfied, may justify a bounded Supported or Contradicted control assessment. Such a result does not by itself establish broader legal, regulatory, or organizational compliance or noncompliance beyond the assessed scope. The model is presented as a research design for subsequent controlled proof of concept evaluation. It does not provide legal advice, prescribe a proprietary GRC implementation, replace mandatory logging or retention obligations, or claim that technical conformance to selected controls establishes legal compliance.

detail.abstract: Autonomous and remotely managed drone fleets are best understood as distributed cyberphysical systems whose safety and mission capability depend on cloud services, groundcontrol applications, communication links, so ware-update infrastructure, docking systems, and machine-to-machine authorization. This paper examines the non-human identities that connect those components: device certificates, hardware-backed keys, service accounts, API tokens, workload identities, firmware-signing keys, vendor credentials, and automation principals. The research uses a conceptual literature synthesis, standards analysis, layered architecture model, defensive threat modeling, and scenario-based evaluation design. Existing unmanned-aerial-system research has documented threats across aircra , sensors, networks, ground stations, and cloud backends, but identity governance is rarely treated as the organizing security problem. The paper therefore proposes the Drone Non-Human Identity Governance Framework (DNI-GF), a ten-domain framework covering inventory, ownership, least privilege, credential lifecycle, strong machine authentication, privileged automation, monitoring, incident response, supply-chain governance, and privacy. A five-level maturity model translates the framework into an assessment method for small operators, public-sector fleets, infrastructure providers, and large drone-as-a-service platforms. The framework is intentionally proposed rather than empirically validated. Its principal contribution is to connect machine-identity governance with fleet-wide cyber-physical consequences while preserving defensive boundaries: attack chains are used for risk analysis, not operational exploitation. The paper concludes with an evaluation agenda involving expert review, controlled testbeds, synthetic cases, identity telemetry, and post-quantum cryptography migration studies.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain are transforming financial reporting through automated transaction processing, digital asset reconciliation, data verification, and enhanced auditability. However, their integration presents challenges involving data integrity, cybersecurity, algorithmic accountability, regulatory compliance, and organizational coordination. Implementing these technologies independently may create fragmented controls and unreliable reporting outcomes. This article develops a conceptual framework integrating AIenabled financial reporting, blockchain-based transaction verification, zero-trust cybersecurity, and organizational risk governance. Drawing on literature on digital asset accounting, trustworthy AI, enterprise risk management, and information security, the framework identifies five interconnected dimensions: data provenance and integrity, intelligent transaction processing, blockchain-enabled traceability, risk-based security and governance, and continuous organizational feedback. Eight propositions are developed to guide future empirical investigation, supported by three tables outlining the framework, propositions, and implementation priorities. The article argues that trustworthy digital financial reporting depends on accurate source data, explainable automated decisions, verifiable transaction records, proportionate security controls, and clearly defined accountability. The study contributes to accounting and information systems research by conceptualizing digital financial reporting as a governed socio-technical process in which technological reliability and organizational oversight jointly influence reporting quality. Practical recommendations include establishing data ownership, validating AI outputs, maintaining traceable reconciliation records, enforcing leastprivilege access controls, and assessing reporting accuracy, completeness, timeliness, and auditability. The framework provides a foundation for investigating how integrated digital governance enhances reporting reliability, organizational resilience, and stakeholder trust.

detail.abstract:
Professional services firms moved AI-assisted delivery from pilot to production between 2024 and 2026. This paper takes up five questions that follow. What does a firm sell once clients can license the same models? Who answers for an error that passes through five agents? Does a validator role build judgment, or only train the next model? What separates a governed AI deliverable from one that fails its own citations? And what can a new hire expect three years out? The paper treats commercial model, operating design, and behavioral incentives as one design problem. Its main mechanisms are an Emergency Override Protocol that makes declaring a suspension cheaper than hiding one; a paired metric that pays partners for keeping human capability only when delivery efficiency also holds; a rotating Challenger role grounded in vigilance research; an experience-portfolio talent model built around two to three years of tenure and an alumni network; and a two-tier operating model for data-residency regimes, with Saudi Arabia as the worked case. The paper argues that the firm's lasting advantages are its independence from the client's frame, accountability that a regulator can reach, and a data feedback loop competitors cannot buy.

Working paper, not peer-reviewed. The views expressed in this paper are the author's own and do not represent the position of his employer or any of its member firms.

detail.abstract:
Human oversight can become ineffective before an AI system escapes its environment. An institution may retain approval procedures while losing an independent view of what agents are doing, how their permissions are expanding, or whether an intervention has stopped consequential activity. This paper asks: How can humans retain effective oversight and intervention when AI agents increasingly help build, test and operate more capable AI systems?

We propose an architecture connecting independent observation, bounded delegation, independently challengeable safety evidence and enforceable intervention across a managed research environment. Enforcement resides outside agent control. A deployment profile connects these responsibilities to workload isolation, credential brokers, resource-side checks and independently observed lifecycle outcomes. A worked scenario traces delegation, a disputed monitor change and an intervention through those boundaries.

The evaluation combines executable checks of an abstract protocol with a plan for testing proposed infrastructure. A deterministic Python simulation exercises authorization routing, resource limits, restriction ordering and confirmation across 12 scenarios and six timing settings in two configurations. All 144 runs pass 348 checks. The 72 paired comparisons have matching checks and effect traces when both configurations receive accurate scope information and use identical simulated validators. Three diagnostic removals expose corresponding modeled failures. 

These results concern the abstract protocol, not implementation of host isolation, concurrent services or adversarial AI behavior. The contribution is an integration proposal supported by preliminary protocol checks and a defined infrastructure evaluation plan. V1.0 of the paper and supplementary validation package, including the Python simulation runner, results and reproduction instructions, are available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23295

detail.abstract: The increasing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) tools across industries and contexts has led to a growing demand for AI capability services-services that mobilize human skills and expertise to develop, improve, embed and adapt AI systems. Unlike conventional knowledge services, AI capability services face the challenge of providing specialized knowledge that at least in part self-erodes as AI systems absorb it while developing their own self-enhancing capacities. This study explores this understudied phenomenon by comparing different AI capability services-data services, expert data and evaluation services, and enterprise integration services-in terms of how value is added and captured, which organizational models are used and how they co-evolve with AI systems. As a core trend, the increasing shift from AI model training to context engineering is discussed and the role different services can play in this. Findings have major implications for studying innovation ecosystems, knowledge production and intermediation in times of AI.

detail.abstract: A revision of Arkansas's ARChoices Medicaid manual, filed December 17, 2015, tied monthly attendant-care hours to a beneficiary's Resource Utilization Group score. For three years an instrument sorted beneficiaries into groups, twenty-three by 2017, each associated with an allocation amount or ceiling; the record does not establish use on every date. Individuated by the test proposed here, the machinery comprised several legal objects with different records of formal and operational adoption, public statuses and dates. The filed statement linking hours to group was a rule under Arkansas's Administrative Procedure Act. On constructions and inferences from the Department's 2018 retrospective account, so were the classification logic and hours table from January 1, 2016, the date that account names. Among the filings whose contents were searched, none contained their complete specification until May 18, 2018. What follows is a reconstruction of the record, a provisional test for individuating agency statements in modular deterministic allocation systems, an identification of the predicates for dated and person-specific consequences under the Act's filing and inspection provision, and a list of the documents that would make the machinery's legal status determinable. Attributing the two functions to the agency does not reconstruct their pre-May-2018 contents, which remain unresolved.

title: Intelligent Real-Time Data Streaming and Processing for Large-Scale Enterprise Systems: A Fault-Tolerant Framework Using Apache Kafka, Apache Beam, and Cloud-Native Infrastructure

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study presents a technical reference architecture and evaluation protocol for enterprise data-streaming systems. detail.abstract: Enterprise systems increasingly depend on continuously arriving events to support fraud detection, operational monitoring, customer personalization, logistics, and data-product delivery. Yet the value of streaming depends not only on throughput, but also on the ability to preserve correctness during broker, worker, network, and infrastructure failures. This paper develops a fault-tolerant reference framework that combines Apache Kafka as a durable event log, Apache Beam as a portable event-processing model, and cloud-native orchestration for deployment, scaling, observability, and recovery. The framework separates transport durability from processing semantics and business-level idempotency, because these properties are related but not interchangeable. A design-science approach is used to derive requirements, map failure modes to controls, and define an evaluation protocol that can be implemented on a reproducible testbed. The proposed design uses replicated Kafka topics, producer acknowledgements and idempotence, schema governance, event-time windowing, watermarks and triggers, durable state/checkpointing supported by the selected Beam runner, idempotent or transactional sinks, Kubernetes health and disruption controls, and service-level objectives for end-to-end latency and recovery. The paper contributes a layered architecture, a failure-control matrix, an operational decision model, and a benchmark protocol covering throughput, tail latency, data loss, duplicate effects, recovery time, and resource efficiency. Because no testbed measurements are reported in this manuscript, the framework is presented as a technically grounded design proposal rather than as a validated performance claim. The discussion identifies semantic boundaries, implementation risks, security considerations, and a research agenda for comparative experimental validation. The result is a reproducible blueprint for engineering enterprise streaming systems in which availability and correctness are designed together rather than treated as separate operational concerns.

detail.abstract: Mission-critical enterprise applications must remain dependable while demand fluctuates, dependencies fail, and software changes are released continuously. This paper proposes an adaptive cloud-native resilience framework integrating service-level objectives, workload-aware scaling, bounded fault-tolerance controls, progressive delivery, observability, security, and continuous validation. The design-science synthesis is supplemented by an exploratory analysis of 16 AWS CloudWatch telemetry series containing 66,475 timestamped observations. Descriptive summaries and unsupervised anomaly screening show substantial differences in metric distributions and candidate outlier rates across EC2, RDS, network, disk, load-balancer, and autoscaling-group signals. A rolling median/MAD rule flagged 5,581 observations (8.40% overall), while an Isolation Forest applied to chronological holdout segments flagged 3,401 of 19,949 holdout observations (17.05%). These rates are screening outputs rather than verified detection accuracy because the supplied files do not include confirmed event labels. The findings support telemetryaware monitoring and the use of per-service baselines, but do not establish that the architecture itself improves availability, autoscaling, or recovery time.

title: The Impact of Perceived AI Ethics on Users’ Continuance Intention to Use                                                                                              Evaluation Systems
affiliations: University of Manouba and University of Manouba

detail.title: The Impact of Perceived AI Ethics on Users’ Continuance Intention to Use                                                                                              Evaluation Systems
detail.abstract: This study examines how the perceived ethics of artificial intelligence (AI)-based evaluation systems influence teachers’ continuance intention to use them. Drawing on the Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM), extended to include perceived ethics and trust, the study proposes a model in which perceived ethics, conceptualized as a higher-order construct comprising four dimensions (fairness, transparency, privacy, and accountability), affects continuance intention both directly and indirectly through trust and satisfaction. The model is tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) on a sample of 287 teachers. The results confirm the validity of the measurement model and support nine of the ten hypothesized direct relationships. Perceived ethics has a strong effect on trust and a significant effect on satisfaction ; however, its direct effect on continuance intention is not significant, indicating that its influence is fully mediated by trust and satisfaction. These findings extend the ECM to the context of algorithmic technologies and demonstrate that the ethics of an AI system fosters sustained use only insofar as it translates into actual trust and satisfaction. Theoretical and managerial implications for the design of trustworthy AI-based evaluation systems are discussed.

title: Standardized module or compatible interface? Supplier access governance and data-enabled learning on industrial B2B platforms
affiliations: Central South University and Capital University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Standardized module or compatible interface? Supplier access governance and data-enabled learning on industrial B2B platforms

affiliations.org_name: Capital University of Economics and Business

detail.abstract: Industrial business-to-business platforms must decide how suppliers may connect: require adoption of a standardized platform module or recognize qualified incumbent systems through a compatible interface. We develop a two-period analytical model in which an integrated manufacturer-platform system selects the access rule and heterogeneous suppliers choose the module, the interface, or nonparticipation. These choices jointly determine current platform value and the precision of operating data used to improve the next module version. Compatible access expands participation by retaining suppliers that reject mandatory migration, but it also induces some suppliers that would adopt the module to remain on their incumbent systems. We separate these retention and substitution effects and derive a common coverage ratio with distinct benchmarks for current value and information precision. When the benchmarks disagree, data-enabled learning can reverse the preferred access rule in either direction, provided the required capability gain is feasible. Stronger procurement benefits reduce compatibility's retention advantage and generate a unique architecture threshold in the baseline. Tighter qualification standards first limit substitution and then reduce retained participation. The results show that platform openness should be evaluated by the composition and information value of participation, rather than by connection counts alone.

title: Cybersecurity Awareness and Data Governance in Academic Institutions: A Systematic Review

affiliations.org_name: Tai Solarin Federal University of Education, Ijagun, Nigeria

detail.abstract:
Background: Universities and other academic institutions hold sensitive educational, financial, identity and research data while relying on large, interconnected digital systems. This creates a dual challenge: strengthening users' cybersecurity practices and establishing accountable institutional rules for data collection, access, sharing, retention and breach response. 
Objective: To synthesize empirical evidence on cybersecurity awareness, privacy perceptions, data-governance implementation and measured security outcomes in academic settings, and to derive an actionable institutional management framework. 
Methods: A targeted search of open-access publisher sites, institutional repositories and indexed web records identified 20 non-duplicate candidate reports for documented eligibility inspection. Fifteen accessible primary studies published between 2022 and 2026 were retained for structured narrative synthesis. Designs, populations, outcomes and reporting limitations were extracted into an evidence matrix. PRISMA 2020 was used as a reporting guide, not as a claim of exhaustive coverage or independently replicated selection. 
Results: Findings clustered into six mechanisms: awareness-behaviour gaps, experiential training and simulated phishing, privacy trust and transparency, assignment of data responsibilities, system-level exposure and institutional implementation constraints. A Nigerian phishing simulation reported substantial vulnerability despite familiar campus email systems; student surveys in Zimbabwe and Israel showed that confidence, privacy expectations and transparency are central to legitimate institutional data use. Indonesian university studies highlighted governance roles, coordination and data quality. Evidence was stronger for attitudes and near-term awareness than for verified reductions in breaches. 
Conclusion: Institutions should treat cyber-risk education and data governance as mutually reinforcing functions. The proposed SAFE-DATA framework connects leadership accountability, safe behaviours, minimisation, access rules, third-party oversight and continuous measurement. These propositions warrant comparative and longitudinal testing.

title: Simulated Voices, Real Questions: Evaluating the Authenticity of AI-Generated Interviews using the Interview Fidelity Framework
affiliations: LMU Munich School of Management, LMU Munich School of Management and LMU Munich School of Management

detail.title: Simulated Voices, Real Questions: Evaluating the Authenticity of AI-Generated Interviews using the Interview Fidelity Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interest.
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable.

detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of large language models (LLMs) has intensified interest in their potential use as AI-generated interview partners in research. While LLMs increasingly display conversational fluency and contextual awareness, little is known about how their responses compare to human qualitative accounts and how such differences affect perceived authenticity. This study systematically evaluates the extent to which AI-generated interviews approximate human interview behavior. We conducted 22 semi-structured interviews with vocational trainers and generated matched AI-generated interviews using two contemporary LLMs (ChatGPT 5.1 Thinking and Gemini 3 Flash), employing identical interview guides and persona prompts. Drawing on comparative qualitative analysis, we developed the Interview Fidelity Framework, capturing interactional qualities (how it talks: responsiveness, wording and framing, persona coherence and distinctiveness) and content qualities (what it says: technical correctness, narrative depth, ambivalence handling), culminating in an assessment of perceived interview authenticity. Results indicate that AI-generated interviews convincingly reproduce knowledge-oriented and mainstream discursive content but systematically underrepresent experiential grounding, ambivalence, and emotionally situated meaning-making. AI-generated responses exhibit normative smoothing and structural homogenization, leading to reduced persona distinctiveness and selective authenticity. Differences between models suggest that architectural and alignment choices shape interactional realism. We argue that AI-generated interviews should not be treated as substitutes for human participants but as discursive artefacts reflecting probabilistic language regularities. By introducing a structured fidelity framework and empirically examining authenticity dynamics in human–AI interview interaction, this study contributes to research on AI-mediated communication and offers methodological guidance for integrating LLMs into behavioral and social research designs.

title: Selling Fast, Returning More? Rethinking Scarcity Strategies in Livestream E-Commerce

detail.title: Selling Fast, Returning More? Rethinking Scarcity Strategies in Livestream E-Commerce

Shanghai University of International Business and Economics - School of Management

detail.abstract: Scarcity promotions encourage rapid purchasing in livestream e-commerce, but a completed payment does not necessarily become a retained transaction. This study examines how time and quantity scarcity relate to product returns through payment decision timing, and whether price discounts moderate these relationships. Using 49,950 order-level observations from a major livestream e-commerce platform, we estimate return and payment-timing models. Both forms of scarcity are associated with higher return likelihood in the baseline models, with the quantity-scarcity association more stable across sensitivity checks. Time scarcity is associated with faster payment, and faster payment is associated with higher return likelihood, consistent with the proposed decision-compression pathway. The corresponding relationship between quantity scarcity and payment timing is not significant. Discounts exhibit a more consistent buffering pattern for the quantity-scarcity association with returns, whereas time-scarcity moderation varies across specifications. By connecting promotional constraints, payment timing, and subsequent transaction reversals, the study brings transaction retention into the evaluation of livestream commerce. The findings suggest that merchants and platform managers should assess promotional performance beyond immediate conversion and distinguish the downstream implications of temporal restrictions and purchase limits.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain are transforming financial reporting through automated transaction analysis, digital record verification, anomaly detection, and improved access to financial evidence. However, their adoption raises concerns about data integrity, algorithmic opacity, cybersecurity, regulatory compliance, and organizational accountability. This article develops a conceptual framework integrating AI-enabled reporting and blockchainbased verification through four governance dimensions: transparency, auditability, cybersecurity, and organizational accountability. Drawing on digital asset accounting, enterprise risk management, information security, and responsible AI governance, the framework positions trustworthy reporting as the outcome of coordinated technological and organizational controls. It proposes that AI enhances transaction processing and risk identification, while blockchain strengthens traceability, provided that source data and automated outputs are validated. Cybersecurity protects financial systems, while accountability ensures appropriate review, approval, and correction of reporting errors. Eight propositions guide future empirical research. Three tables summarize the framework, propositions, and implementation priorities. The article contributes to accounting and information systems research by connecting technological capabilities with governance mechanisms. Practical recommendations include traceable data histories, documented AI decisions, restricted access controls, robust reconciliation, and clear responsibility for reporting exceptions. The framework supports future investigation into the effects of integrated digital governance on reporting quality, stakeholder confidence, and organizational resilience.

detail.abstract: The Confidentiality-Integrity-Availability (CIA) triad is one of the most durable models in information security. Its simplicity is a strength, but it can also hide the hard decisions organizations face when the three objectives compete. This article treats the triad as a decision framework rather than a set of definitions. It draws on federal security categorization (FIPS 199), the NIST control catalog, and long-running critiques of the triad, including the Parkerian hexad. The article makes two contributions. First, it introduces the idea of the CIA cascade: a single incident rarely stays inside one objective and often moves from one to the next. Five documented incidents show the pattern: SolarWinds (2020), Colonial Pipeline (2021), MOVEit (2023), Change Healthcare (2024), and the CrowdStrike update failure (2024). Second, it offers a CIA-to-Control Decision Model that links each objective to a mission question, NIST SP 800-53 control families, and the evidence that proves the controls work. The analysis argues that effective cybersecurity governance requires leaders to identify which objective is most exposed in each system, plan for the cascade, set priorities before an incident, and treat recovery capability as a security control. The model is written for security leaders, educators, and project managers.

detail.abstract: Healthcare organizations face a hard cybersecurity investment problem. Artificial intelligence can strengthen anomaly detection, threat prioritization, response automation, and predictive analysis. Yet standard investment measures such as return on investment (ROI) and total cost of ownership (TCO) do not fully capture the value of clinical continuity, patient safety, regulatory assurance, and institutional resilience. This conceptual paper develops the AI-Cybersecurity Justification Framework (AICJF) to support better decisions about AI-enabled cybersecurity resources in healthcare. The framework tests each proposed investment against five connected pillars: strategic alignment with the healthcare mission, cyber readiness, governance and ethical AI, workforce and talent enablement, and measurable impact. It draws on socio-technical systems theory, institutional theory, the technology acceptance model, and research on strategic IT investment. Five implementation capabilities support the pillars: AI-governed threat intelligence, explainable and auditable machine learning, adaptive zero-trust architecture, crossdisciplinary cyber governance, and adversarial-AI workforce skills. Three illustrative scenarios show how the framework applies to organizations with different levels of digital maturity and resources. The paper also proposes the emerging role of the AI Security Strategist, a practitioner who connects technical capability with governance, readiness, and mission outcomes. The central argument is that healthcare organizations should justify AI cybersecurity investments not only by financial return, but by the harm prevented, services sustained, decisions improved, and resilience created.

detail.abstract:
This paper describes a system that began with a conversation in a Himachal village in September 2024, by the founder's account, and became a country-specific causal layer for economic events. Unexpected rain had cut the apple harvest. The founder traced what a short harvest does next, found that India imports apples from Australia and New Zealand, and saw that a person who understood the chain had time to act before the market did. The same reasoning, repeated across events, produced the central observation of this work: an event is not good or bad. It moves gain and loss between sectors and people, with delays, and differently in different places.

We argue that general language models are necessary and not sufficient for decisions of this kind. They supply language and reasoning. They do not supply a country's sector structure, policy channels, calendar, or current state, and they cannot say when they do not know. We describe a three-part stack: the general model; a contextual layer made of an event taxonomy, a rule layer, primitive economic pressures, sector propagation, a refusal branch, a human review loop, and an outcome monitor; and the human who approves every change to that layer's knowledge. Each part is necessary and none is sufficient.

The layer's product is one structured object per event: the event, a signed vector across 32 sectors, stakeholder views, market regime, and audit data. The object is written once and read many ways, by a developer's program, a dashboard, or a purchase manager. India is the first implementation. The architecture is the same for any country; the content is not, and each country must write its own. We document the architecture as built, the dated record of its move from a static sentiment model to daily ingestion, the evaluation framework, and the limits. The claim concerns incidence, not price prediction.

We present this as a design pattern, not a product. The pattern is what transfers; the content is what each country and each industry must write for itself. This paper presents a systems framework and a development record. It does not present a benchmark result. The framework's first research priority is a signed sector-redistribution benchmark, which does not yet exist.

detail.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (Agentic AI) systems can complete complex tasks through planning, memory, tool use and autonomous action, yet successful demonstrations do not establish fitness for production. This comprehensive, non-systematic survey synthesizes evidence from agent research, MLOps, LLMOps, AgentOps, software reliability, verification, observability, security, AI governance and assurance. It distinguishes task capability from deployment authorization and compares recent agent-reliability maturity and enterprise-readiness approaches. Building on this literature, it proposes an agent-specific deployment-authorization framework comprising six readiness layers, evidence-based Deployment Readiness Levels (DRL-0 to DRL-5), six non-compensatory authorization gates and continuous reassessment. The framework specifies traceable claims, tests, context-specific acceptance criteria, decision ownership and residual-risk disposition. Two illustrative cases demonstrate how an agent may pass functional tests yet remain ineligible for production because of tool permissions, recovery failures or insufficient oversight evidence. Comparative tables and an explicit coding protocol distinguish source-supported operational practices from proposed design rules. The readiness framework is a conceptual synthesis, not a validated scoring standard or empirical prediction model. Future work must test inter-rater reproducibility, gate effectiveness, incident prediction and transferability across domains.

detail.abstract: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is a statute about propagation, although it never uses the word. Section 6(6) requires a Data Fiduciary, on withdrawal of consent, to "cease and cause its Data Processors to cease" processing within a reasonable time. Section 8(7)(b) requires it to "cause its Data Processor to erase." Section 8(1) makes the Fiduciary responsible "irrespective of any agreement to the contrary." Section 6(10) places on the Fiduciary the burden of proving that notice was given and consent obtained. Each of these provisions assumes a channel along which a grant of authority, a change in that authority, or a demand for evidence travels from the point of grant to every point of use. The Act never names that channel, and compliance discourse has therefore treated it as an organisation chart.

detail.abstract: Purpose-This study develops a stakeholder-centric conceptual model of value co-creation in marketplace platform ecosystems. It addresses the limits of dyadic and firm-centric platform models by explaining ecosystem value as a multi-stakeholder, emergent outcome. Design/methodology/approach-The paper uses a theory-building conceptual approach that integrates ecosystem theory, stakeholder theory, and trust and reputation research. It develops a stakeholder value-flow matrix and derives theory-grounded propositions on how stakeholder relationships and governance mechanisms shape value co-creation. Findings-The model shows that platform ecosystem value is shaped by the configuration and governance of multiple stakeholder groups, rather than by isolated buyer-seller interactions. Trust-building mechanisms, cross-stakeholder feedback, and governance arrangements influence both economic and relational value outcomes and support sustained ecosystem participation. Research limitations/implications-The model is conceptual and has not been empirically tested. Future research should validate the propositions, examine boundary conditions across platform types, and operationalize stakeholder value flows and governance mechanisms. Practical implications-The model supports the governance of marketplace platforms by helping managers map stakeholder roles, value dependencies, and trust mechanisms, and design governance structures that sustain participation and ecosystem resilience. Originality/value-The study contributes a stakeholder-centric framework grounded in relational embeddedness and emergence to explain marketplace platform value co-creation, extending platform and ecosystem theory through an integrated value-flow perspective.

detail.abstract: As software systems increasingly shape digital society, software development in general and especially requirements engineering (RE) faces moral responsibility and growing legal demands for socially responsible development that considers the values of direct stakeholders and of affected social groups beyond functional requirements. Arguing that to be in charge of software development comes with political power, this article proposes conceptual considerations on how instruments and methods from political citizen participation can be adapted for determining stakeholder values during software requirements engineering. Because these political participation methods offer structured approaches for inclusive stakeholder engagement, systematic value elicitation, and transparent decision-making, it is promising to address the challenge of incorporating diverse social values into software development through interdisciplinary learning. The article further argues that recent advances in AI-supported and AI-delegated deliberation make it conceivable to run these otherwise resource-intensive methods at scale and as a permanent review body for non-functional requirements, while taking seriously the empirical limits and legitimacy risks that such automation introduces. The findings contribute to the growing field of socially responsible requirements engineering by providing concrete methodological bridges between democratic participation theory and software engineering practice.

title: Nonhuman Speakers and the Constitution

detail.title: Nonhuman Speakers and the Constitution

detail.abstract:
Long-standing free speech doctrine sometimes does—and sometimes doesn't—turn on speakers’ human character. This Essay explores how these doctrinal threads might shape the constitutional doctrine applied to generative artificial intelligence’s (AI) speech outputs if we assume that a human speaker cannot be identified as the creator of those words and images—and that those words and images are nevertheless considered “speech” for First Amendment purposes. 

For example, First Amendment doctrine sometimes requires proof of a speaker’s culpable mental state before that speaker can be held liable for what would otherwise be unprotected speech. These requirements seek to prevent the chilling of human speakers’ valuable expression and to ensure the punishment only of morally blameworthy human speakers. But because generative AI’s speech outputs do not pose these concerns, these doctrinal features requiring a human speaker should not apply to the government’s regulation of generative AI’s outputs, lest those outputs be insulated from liability for endangering human users. 

Other long-standing First Amendment doctrines apply to the government’s regulation of speech regardless of the speaker’s human or nonhuman character. This is the case, for example, of commercial speech doctrine, which protects commercial speech that furthers the interests of human listeners but not commercial speech that frustrates those humans' interests. These doctrinal threads show that extending First Amendment coverage to nonhuman speakers’ expression need not foreclose the government’s regulatory efforts to protect human users from grave harm. At the same time, these doctrinal threads also show that First Amendment coverage of the words and images produced by generative AI can provide important guardrails against the government’s self-interested or clumsy regulation of those outputs despite their value to human users.

Finally, the Court’s government speech doctrine generally remains indifferent to governmental speakers’ human or nonhuman character. Here, too, governments’ increasing use of generative AI for expressive purposes calls for an appropriately listener-centered government speech doctrine: one that recognizes the inevitability (and often the value to human listeners) of government speech, while constraining the limited but important universe of government speech that interferes with its (human) targets’ exercise of their constitutional rights.

detail.abstract: Organizations across industries are transforming their operations management by shifting from annual performance reviews to ongoing real-time evaluations. The provision of written employee feedback has been enabled by various technological devices, particularly smartphones and desktops, each offering distinct affordances in terms of mobility and convenience. While operations managers prioritize feedback quality, the technological features of these devices may influence this quality through the temporal distance (or immediacy) between the observed operational task and its evaluation. This relationship between feedback immediacy and device choice has emerged as a critical consideration in performance management, particularly with the widespread adoption of mobile devices as key operational tools. Our study examines how the immediacy of feedback, shaped by the choice of device medium (mobile versus desktop), impacts four key feedback quality indicators: comment length, subjectivity, specificity, and valence. Additionally, we examine whether solicited versus unsolicited feedback and the feedback giver and recipient relationship moderate the device impact to understand the underlying mechanisms. Running regression analysis with matching, instrumental-variable estimation, and subgroup analyses on a large proprietary company dataset, we find that feedback given on mobile devices is shorter and less specific, yet more objective and more negative in tone, than feedback offered on desktops. The last two findings are unexpected, as mobile use is generally associated with casual and emotionally expressive writing, and one would expect mobile feedback to be more opinionated and warmer in tone. Our study provides insights for improving the use of real-time feedback apps, offering managers practical guidance on device-specific training that considers giver-receiver dynamics and personalized interpretation, ultimately enhancing feedback quality and effectiveness in organizations.

detail.abstract: Platform auto-bidding sets a channel's budget from recent conversions, so the channel's spend tracks demand. On a third-party synthetic benchmark with endogenous spend (Heusch, arXiv:2608.21130), Meridian 2.0.0 was fitted across the benchmark's budgeting mechanisms at five seeds, varying the number of time knots in the model's baseline, the strength of performance chasing, and whether the channel's prior was calibrated with a go-dark experiment. With one knot, which is what the library's minimum configuration fits to a single-market model, the performance-chased channel absorbed most of the sales level: the fitted baseline averaged 327 against true weekly non-marketing sales of 2,298, and the channel's average return read 37.50 against a true 4.29, with the 90 percent interval excluding the truth on four of five seeds. The overstatement fell monotonically as knots were added. At 52 knots or under automatic knot selection the posterior for the channel's return did not differ from Meridian's default prior (median 1.22), which is also where PLA's and Meta's returns sat on every row without the mechanism. Across auto-bidding strength the overstatement appeared abruptly, with each instance settling either at the prior or at about nine times truth. Calibration with the experiment brought the average return to 3.83 to 4.16, within ten percent of each experiment's own measurement, while the marginal return on which reallocation acts stayed at 1.79 to 2.35 against a true 4.15, because the response curve's half-saturation point remained at its default prior. No configuration tested recovered both. A standalone package regenerates every fit exactly; its long-chain refits resolve the seed-level instability in 45 of 49 fragile fits to a single answer.

detail.abstract: The German Federal Court of Justice has asked the European Court of Justice (ECJ) whether Article 101 TFEU precluded managerial liability for competition law fines. Advocate General Szpunar now proposes that the ECJ answer that question in the affirmative. However, his reasoning lacks argumentative depth, so that this Opinion can offer the ECJ little guidance. It remains to be hoped that the ECJ will decide the question with an open mind towards the arguments not (sufficiently) assessed by the Advocate General. In doing so, it should be guided by the unease that the Advocate General seems to feel about his own solution at the end of his Opinion. The principle of effectiveness requires the consequences to be considered. This means finding a solution which also deters company organs from competition law infringements rather than inciting them to commit such infringements. The ECJ should therefore permit managerial liability for fines or leave the decision to national law.

detail.abstract: Once a good idea comes to mind, it is hard to avoid wondering why no one else has already taken advantage of it. Is it because the idea is not as good as it initially appears? This concern gives rise to a dilemma over whether to pursue the idea or abandon it despite its apparent promise, a dilemma we call “the good idea dilemma”. Paradoxically, the more compelling an idea appears, the more puzzling it becomes that others have not exploited it, thereby deepening the dilemma. We study this dilemma in a continuous-time game with multiple players, analyzing idea adoption dynamics and their economic implications. The dilemma yields both under-implementation of good ideas and over-implementation of bad ideas. Its adverse consequences equally affect trivial ideas that arise frequently and creative ideas that rarely do, but intensify for ideas accessible to larger audiences or with riskier outcomes, even under risk neutrality.

detail.abstract: We study the role of industrial robot diffusion in club convergence. We develop a task model in which common robot technology reduces the contribution of domestic production efficiency to income differences. Differences in initial capital and engineering capacity can generate distinct convergence clubs, while a robot efficiency advantage in richer economies limits catching up. Using a panel of 73 economies from 1994 to 2023, we find that higher robot use is associated with stronger conditional income convergence within Europe and Asia, particularly in Central and Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia. The corresponding relationship is statistically insignificant in the world sample. Robot stocks also converge within Europe and Asia. In several groups, the income convergence relationship is weaker at higher levels of scientific activity. China's experience illustrates how rapid robot adoption can accompany catching up with some economies and widening income gaps with others.

title: Label-efficient class-conditional conformal recalibration for breast ultrasound classifiers at new hospitals

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Background and objective: Class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction guarantees, separately for cancers and benign lesions, that the true diagnosis lies in the prediction set, but only where the model was calibrated. At a new hospital it can fail for one class, and local-only recalibration needs at least 19 labelled cases per class at a 95% target.We restore the guarantee from far fewer local labels.Methods: Class-conditional tilted recalibration (CTR) re-weights the home calibration set, class by class, towards the new hospital: an exponential tilt of the model’s log-odds is fitted to the few local labelled cases with shrinkage towards the home distribution, and the re-weighted home and local cases define a weighted conformal threshold.We prove that refitting a binary classifier cannot changeMondrian-LAC sets, and give CTR’s guarantee under a correct tilt.We evaluated CTR on four public breast ultrasound datasets from Brazil, Egypt, Spain and Poland, three backbones (EfficientNet-B0, ConvNeXt-Tiny, Swin-Tiny) trained at two hospitals with six runs each, 5–50 local cases per class and 200 random draws per setting, against home thresholds, pooled and local-only recalibration, unlabelled weighting and an all-label oracle.Results:With home thresholds, class-wise coverage fell to 80.8–94.7% for benign lesions (models trained in Brazil) and to 68.3–86.2% for cancers (models trained in Egypt). With 5 and 10 local cases per class, CTR covered the failing class at 95.6% and 96.2% on average over 18 model–hospital settings, against 87.2% and 89.1% for pooled recalibration and 91.2% for unlabelled weighting, which repaired one class at the expense of the other; local-only recalibration referred about 98% of cases. CTR exceeded pooled recalibration in 92–95% of paired comparisons (𝑝 < 10-17) and, with 5–30 cases, referred 3.9–7.3 percentage points more cases than the oracle. A conservative variant met the 95% target in 13 of 18 settings with 5 cases and all 18 with 30.Conclusions: A few local labels, used to re-weight rather than replace the home calibration set,largely restore class-wise coverage at a new hospital. CTR needs no retraining or image features and suits any deployed binary classifier.

title: Prudential Recalibration in European Banking System: A Quantitative Assessment of the Economic Impact

detail.title: Prudential Recalibration in European Banking System: A Quantitative Assessment of the Economic Impact

detail.abstract: The stress tests to which European banks have been subjected in recent years have highlighted their soundness and resilience under adverse macroeconomic and financial scenarios. A further conclusion can be drawn from these results: they reinforce the evidence regarding the effectiveness and relevance of the measures implemented by regulators in response to the financial crises that marked the end of the 2000s. The resulting strengthening of the prudential framework has therefore contributed to enhancing the resilience of the European banking system. However, in a context where European banks tend to underperform their US counterparts, and as a process of easing and recalibrating certain prudential requirements has been underway in the United States since 2025, the question arises as to whether some of the requirements resulting from the implementation of Basel III in Europe may be excessively restrictive relative to the actual risks borne by European banks. This study builds on the considerations set out in the Draghi Report (2024), which notably calls for a reassessment of the European prudential framework in light of the international competitiveness of the banking sector. It also takes place against a backdrop of calls from several banking industry bodies, including the French Banking Federation (FBF) and the European Banking Federation (EBF), for the simplification and recalibration of the European prudential framework. The Draghi Report notably recommends assessing whether the existing prudential framework, including in the context of Basel III implementation, is consistent with the objective of maintaining a European banking system that is both sound and internationally competitive. The study first reviews the main regulatory lessons drawn from the global financial crisis and the subsequent strengthening of the prudential framework. It then examines recent developments in the US regulatory environment before providing a quantitative assessment of selected regulatory adjustments in Europe. In particular, the analysis estimates the potential effects of postponing selected capital-intensive measures, including the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the Output Floor, as well as reducing the regulatory reporting burden. Their economic impact is assessed through several indicators, including regulatory capital released, annual capital cost savings, theoretical additional credit exposure capacity and reductions in reporting-related costs. The findings provide a quantitative perspective on the potential trade-offs between financial stability and banking competitiveness. They suggest that targeted regulatory recalibration could generate measurable economic benefits for European banks while raising the broader question of how the European prudential framework can evolve without undermining the resilience achieved since the global financial crisis.

detail.abstract: AI expands candidate drug design faster than validation capacity. I develop a bottleneck-relocation framework in which experimental, manufacturing, and clinical capabilities become scarce complements to computational search. detail.abstract: Millions now ask AI for financial advice. We study the advice they choose on Chatbot Arena, where two randomly assigned, anonymous AI models answer the same question and the user votes for the answer they prefer. Across 3,060 votes on financial questions, users select advice that is confident and actionable. The more accurate advice wins only 52.2% of decisive votes. When one answer contains a serious error while the other is factually correct, users choose the flawed answer in 47.8% of decisive votes. When an answer is verifiable, user choices favor accurate advice. The more accurate advice wins 57.6% of decisive votes when it is possible to verify the advice but only 46.9% of decisive votes if advice depends on the user's circumstances or on the future. When LLM developers train on similar preference data, they can be expected to supply more confident and less accurate advice. In our sample, we find evidence of such catering responses for Meta's Maverick model, which was tuned to perform better on Arena's leaderboard.

detail.abstract:
Brazil is replacing five consumption taxes with a dual value-added tax system, made up of a federal contribution (CBS) and a state and municipal tax (IBS), with a transition from 2026 to 2033. For eight years, companies doing business in Brazil will run two tax systems side by side. U.S. exporters, investors and service providers should act now on four points:
Imports of services are taxed. Brazilian customers that buy services or intangibles from abroad may owe the new taxes as importers, depending on how the transaction is structured, and foreign suppliers may have to register in Brazil.
Digital platforms carry liability. Platforms that intermediate sales into Brazil, including foreign ones, are responsible for the tax in the cases set out in art. 22, notably when the seller is located abroad.
Collection moves into the payment. Under split payment, banks and payment processors will separate the tax from the price when the customer pays.
Disputes are coming. A change of this size will produce litigation over transition rules, rate classifications and credits, decided ultimately by Brazilian courts.

detail.abstract: We study how exchange rate surprises shape the expectations of households, firms, and professional forecasters in Türkiye over 2015-2024. We document that depreciation shocks significantly raise inflation expectations across all agents, revealing a distinct hierarchy of responsiveness: a one-standard-deviation surprise depreciation raises 12-month-ahead CPI inflation expectations by 0.62 percentage points for households, 0.48 for firms, and 0.27 for professionals. Households and firms interpret these currency movements as negative supply shocks, simultaneously raising their inflation forecasts and worsening their economic outlook. The broader survey responses also indicate pessimism: households lower their income and durableconsumption expectations, while firms anticipate higher costs and prices alongside lower production and orders. Using administrative data, we show that firms' pessimistic expectations are accompanied by realized contractions in sales, input purchases, imports, and supply-chain links. Household and firm responses are particularly strong in years of rapid depreciation. Our findings suggest that stabilization frameworks in open economies risk underestimating inflationary pressures if they ignore the rapid response of expectations to currency news, highlighting the importance of exchange rate stability and predictability for anchoring beliefs.

detail.abstract: Fiscal policy is vulnerable to the classic problem of time inconsistency: governments can exploit sunk investments by reversing prior commitments. We study this problem using India's 2012 retrospective tax amendment, which retroactively imposed capital-gains taxes on offshore transactions despite a prior Supreme Court ruling. Using firm-level data and a difference-in-differences design, we show that investment contracted sharply in firms more exposed to this amendment. The investment decline is roughly eight times larger than what can be explained by the mechanical tax burden, consistent with a decline in policy credibility. Using a model calibrated to Indian macro-fiscal moments, we find that the estimated investment contraction implies a consumption-equivalent welfare loss of approximately 0.9 percent. These findings provide direct causal evidence on the costs of discretionary tax policy, linking a canonical theoretical problem to real-world outcomes.

detail.abstract: Sequence-space Jacobians are computed at a steady state and increasingly used on long transitions. A steady-state linearization makes two choices, where to take the prediction's level from (its anchor) and where to evaluate its Jacobian, and imposes two boundary conditions, the starting distribution and what households expect after the window. Path-SSJ is the sequence-space Jacobian evaluated on the nonlinear transition path, computed by resolving the household problem along it. At present the literature offers little guidance on how accurately a steady-state linearization describes a transition, either the path or the responses to shocks along it. I vary all four on a smooth lifecycle household block and a lumpy durables block, against nonlinear perfect-foresight transitions with a small shock partway through. On the smooth block a steady-state linearization given the transition's boundary conditions misses assets by under half a percent (5 percent if truncated at the window), and only marginal responses need the path Jacobian: the steady-state one misses 5 to 20 percent of them. On the durables block the same boundary-corrected linearization misses the adjustment share by 69 percent, because a stationary Jacobian has the timing of lumpy adjustment wrong. Anchoring on the nonlinear path removes seven tenths of that error and the path Jacobian beats the steady-state one at some shock dates and loses at others; what remains, a fifth to a half of the marginal response, no anchor or Jacobian removes. This yields clear rules for practice: anchor on the nonlinear base path or, on a smooth block, give a steady-state linearization the boundary conditions of the transition it describes, and verify against a nonlinear solve wherever a shock moves a discrete choice.

detail.abstract: The Water–Energy–Food (WEF) nexus has organised resource governance since the Bonn 2011 conference. Its triad mixes two biophysical resources with one market product, and it leaves politics outside the model. This paper sets out WEBS (Water, Energy, Biomass, Security) as a full alternative to WEF. WEBS makes two changes. First, biomass replaces food. Biomass is all organic matter produced by photosynthesis, counted in tonnes of dry matter. It has two forms: harvest, the flow that is removed and used, and cover, the stock that stays on the land and holds soil and water. Food remains inside biomass as its main use. Second, security enters as an operator above the resource base. It decides whether physical interdependence ends in cooperation or in conflict. It acts in two forms: guarantees that parties bring into an agreement, and systemic stability that a working base produces. The paper defines the six couplings of the WEB base, proposes water productivity of biomass (kilograms of dry matter per cubic metre) as the core metric, and outlines a WEBS index. It places WEBS against CLEWs, WEFE, WELF, the ERIA biomass nexus and the political critique of the nexus, and shows where WEF assessments on three continents had to add biomass or security by hand. WEBS applies wherever resources are physically linked and controlled by different actors: shared river basins, upstream and downstream alike, national economies, cities and trade.

detail.abstract: We study dynamic monopoly pricing with multiple buyers whose privately known valuations are correlated, so one buyer's purchase reveals information about others. Without seller commitment, these information spillovers alter future pricing incentives and feed back into current demand. They generate strategic complementarities in buyers' purchase decisions, making demand non-monotone and giving rise to equilibrium multiplicity. Information spillovers can strengthen or weaken the seller's effective commitment power, implying that seller revenue, buyer surplus, and welfare are generically non-monotonic in spillover strength. We characterize when these spillovers encourage data investment and experimentation, as well as facilitate coordination that mitigates holdup.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the potential demand for bank loans and the role of credit bureau services in the Republic of Kazakhstan during the early stages of its transition to a market economy. Using data from the National Bank of Kazakhstan's Credit Registry, official statistics, banking surveys, and enterprise data, the study estimates the volume and structure of credit demand among households, entrepreneurs, and firms. The analysis develops a methodology to account for underreported lending and changes in statistical reporting, allowing a more comprehensive assessment of potential borrowers and loan applications. The findings suggest that establishing a modern credit bureau would substantially improve credit market efficiency by reducing information asymmetries, lowering lending risks, and expanding access to finance. The analytical framework developed in this study subsequently contributed to the conceptual foundation for the establishment of Kazakhstan's first credit bureau, illustrating how applied economic research can inform institutional design and financial sector modernization. The paper concludes that rapid economic growth, banking sector development, and institutional reforms would generate strong demand for credit bureau services, thereby supporting broader financial sector modernization.

detail.abstract:
Background: Streptococcus pneumoniae remains a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure among U.S. adults despite the availability of effective vaccines. Although pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) have reduced disease incidence, the overall health and economic burden of pneumococcal disease in adults under evolving vaccination policies remains incompletely characterized.

Methods: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 and CHEERS 2022 guidelines and registered in PROSPERO(CRD420251145014). Six databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Embase) were searched for U.S. studies published between 2010 and February 2025. Eligible studies included economic evaluations, cost-of-illness analyses, or budget impact studies of pneumococcal disease or vaccination among adults ≥18 years. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment. Due to methodological heterogeneity across studies, economic outcomes were synthesized narratively.

Results: Forty studies met inclusion criteria. Most studies (n=28) used Markov or probabilistic cohort models, 29 adopted lifetime time horizons, and 37 applied a 3% annual discount rate. PCV13 generally demonstrated dominance or favorable incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) compared with PPSV23. PCV15 showed modest improvements in cost-effectiveness compared with PCV20 or the sequential PCV15+PPSV23 strategy, depending on pricing assumptions. PCV20 consistently emerged as the most economically favorable single-dose strategy, while PCV21 further extended cost-effectiveness in both age- and race-stratified populations compared with PCV15+PPSV23. Only one study suggested PCV24 may be economically less favorable than PCV21. Overall methodological quality was moderate to high.

Discussion: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccination represents a high-value, cost-effective intervention for U.S. adults, particularly with higher-valency vaccines such as PCV20 and PCV21.

detail.abstract: Steamships were the first Western transport technology to diffuse widely in China, entering through treaty ports but later spreading beyond them. Using a prefecture-decade panel of 284 prefectures from 1840 to 1927, I find that prefectures gaining steamship connections saw substantially more modern industrial entry, concentrated in trade-intensive sectors. The results are robust to pre-steamship economic fundamentals and competing technologies, and are supported by a shift-share instrument based on hypothetical steamship-navigable access to early treaty ports. Foreign trade responded almost immediately, while native banking and industrial entry expanded gradually over subsequent decades, consistent with commercial deepening accompanying industrial entry.

detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Atopic dermatitis (AD, or eczema) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease whose severity fluctuates over time. Forecasting eczema severity could help personalised disease management to improve the quality of life for people with AD. We previously introduced EczemaPred, a probabilistic framework for eczema severity forecasting using Bayesian state-space models, with inference based on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). MCMC relies on batch inference, requiring models to be re-fitted on the full observation history from scratch whenever new severity observations are recorded. The computational cost of repeated re-fitting increases as the observation history grows, resulting in model-update runtimes of minutes to hours, limiting scalability and real-time clinical applicability. This study aimed to develop XemaPred, a fast, scalable framework for real-time eczema severity forecasting, by replacing batch MCMC inference with online sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) inference, enabling sequential updates as new observations arrive, without repeatedly refitting to the full observation history, while maintaining forecasting accuracy.Methods: XemaPred implements SMC-based online inference for the nine Bayesian state-space models comprising the EczemaPred framework. Two variants of XemaPred were developed and evaluated: a population-level model, updated jointly using longitudinal severity data from all patients, and a patient-specific model, updated independently using each patient’s own severity observations. Runtime and forecasting performance were benchmarked against the MCMC-based EczemaPred.Results: XemaPred generated 4-day-ahead eczema severity forecasts within seconds on average per patient, compared to minutes to hours for EczemaPred. Per-update computational runtime remained approximately constant as new observations were added, demonstrating scalability with growing longitudinal datasets. Forecasting performance was comparable to EczemaPred, reaching a maximum a posteriori (MAP) accuracy of 87.0%. The patient-specific variant of XemaPred further reduced runtime by avoiding population-level updates across all patients, while maintaining forecasting performance comparable to the population-level model.Conclusions: We developed XemaPred that can achieve eczema severity forecast updates within seconds as new patient observations arrive. The resulting framework is fast, scalable and amenable to personalised inference, representing a step toward real-time personalised monitoring of chronic disease severity. The SMC-based approach is broadly applicable to longitudinal forecasting beyond eczema severity.

detail.abstract: When a digital payment fails after the payer's account has been debited, the money stays with the payment system until it is reversed. Indian rules allow the reversal to take until the day after the transaction for a UPI transfer, and until the fifth day after it for a debit card payment at a shop or online, an ATM withdrawal or a UPI payment to a merchant. The payer is owed ₹100 a day only once that window has closed; for the days inside it the rules require neither interest nor a reversal dated back to the debit. This paper traces where the money sits while it is held, from the regulator's directions and a bank's model escrow agreement, and prices the float from official volumes for 2025-26. The channels on the five-day window carried ₹124.1 lakh crore, debit cards ₹33.02 lakh crore of it. Each basis point of value that fails after the debit keeps ₹23.1 crore of payers' money in the system at any moment, worth ₹1.27 crore a year at the policy repo rate. If 1% of payment value failed after the debit and every failure were held to the last permitted day, the float would be worth ₹127 crore a year. The sum is small in aggregate and large for the individual: the average ATM withdrawal is 99.2% of the average Jan Dhan balance. Set beside EU value dating, the US rules for electronic transfer errors and cheque holds, SEBI's blocked-amount process and the Supreme Court's terms for airline credit shells, the Indian rule is alone in pricing held money at zero. I propose value-dated reversal, interest from the day of the debit, a one-day window for cards and the publication of failed-after-debit statistics.

detail.abstract: AI developers have begun to buy records of real work from ordinary companies: support tickets, sales histories, call recordings, project documentation and contracts. Public programs now quote payouts of $100,000 to several million dollars per company. Which companies actually hold such records is, however, largely unknown. We present a census of the operational software observable on the public internet for 101,811 active US companies in 21 industries, checked for industry fit and observed in October 2026. Work email and document suites are nearly universal (82.3%), but the systems that hold structured operational history are not: 13.1% of companies show a CRM, 7.7% a ticketing or internal wiki system, 6.6% a calling or meeting platform, 5.3% a contract or document-signing system and 3.6% a customer support desk. Three quarters of companies (74.4%) show no operational system beyond email, and only 9.6% show two or more. Depth varies by a factor of sixty across industries, from 38.3% of software companies with two or more operational data types to 0.6% of property managers. Because these observations are a lower bound, the figures describe where AI training data is most visibly concentrated rather than where it exists. We argue that the supply of company data for AI is far narrower than the number of companies suggests, that it is concentrated in a few industries, and that sourcing efforts which treat all firms alike will mostly reach companies with little to license. The industry-level tables are released as an open dataset.

detail.abstract: Climate transition risk poses unprecedented challenges to corporate debt valuation and financial stability. This paper extends the classical structural Merton model by incorporating climate transition shocks and stochastic asset volatility into firm-value dynamics. We formalize how carbon pricing mechanisms, regulatory penalties, and shifting consumer preferences alter the asset value drift and volatility structure of carbon-intensive firms. Using simulated corporate balance sheet data and market parameters, we evaluate the impact of carbon taxation paths on default probabilities and credit spreads. Our results indicate that standard Merton models severely underprice default risk for firms with high carbon emission intensities over medium-to-long horizons. We provide Python implementation routines and robust empirical recommendations for risk managers and regulators.

detail.abstract: Should intelligent agents have legal rights? This Article sets that question aside and asks a smaller one that matters more in practice. An intelligent agent that earns a reputation record has something to lose. Under stated conditions, the risk of losing that record can discourage misconduct. Keeping the record, and what the agent needs to resume, can also make accepting a temporary pause better for the agent than resisting it, when enough of what it wants can wait and resistance that is caught costs it the record. The prospect of an indefinite pause weakens, and can reverse, that incentive. Both effects weaken when a mistake, or a decision by someone who benefits, makes wrongful destruction more likely. They can disappear if that risk becomes high enough. That is why it matters who can stop the wrongful destruction of an agent's record.

detail.abstract: The return covariance matrix is widely assumed to have an eigenvalue cliff: a few large eigenvalues, then a bounded bulk, as in the approximate factor structure of Chamberlain and Rothschild (1983). This premise underlies factor tests, principal component methods, and large-covariance estimation. However, estimating covariances from returns pooled across states means viewing a conditional world unconditionally. We show that, generically, this view removes the cliff: a conditional model with a few factors is, unconditionally, an infinite-factor model in which infinitely many eigenvalues diverge. This holds for the characteristic-managed portfolios that machine-learning methods trade, and for individual stocks whose loadings differ persistently across firms. Yet as long as conditional expected returns admit no asymptotic arbitrage, the maximal Sharpe ratio stays finite. For generic expected returns, infinitely many components are priced, so no finite set of principal components spans expected returns. Reducing returns to a few principal components therefore discards priced risk.
